cau_hoi: What is the basic structural unit of all living organisms?
giai_thich: All organisms, from tiny bacteria to blue whales, are made up of cells. Some organisms consist of a single cell, like bacteria and yeast; others are made up of trillions of cells, like humans. Cells can live, grow, and reproduce on their own. Most cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye and require a microscope to be observed.

cau_hoi: What instrument helps humans see bacteria and tiny cells?
giai_thich: Optical microscopes use lenses to magnify objects hundreds or thousands of times. The electron microscope, invented in 1931, uses a beam of electrons instead of light and can magnify up to millions of times, enough to see viruses. Telescopes and binoculars are used to view distant objects.

cau_hoi: Which tiny organism can cause disease when it enters the body and can be killed by antibiotics?
giai_thich: Bacteria are very small single-celled organisms found everywhere: in soil, water, air, and even in our bodies. Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial, with only a few causing diseases such as tuberculosis, cholera, and typhoid. Antibiotics can kill bacteria but not viruses.

cau_hoi: What organism is used to make yogurt?
giai_thich: Lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus and Streptococcus thermophilus consume lactose in milk and produce lactic acid. The acid causes milk proteins to coagulate, making the milk thick and sour. The acidic environment also prevents harmful bacteria from growing, allowing yogurt to last longer than fresh milk. Pickled vegetables also ferment thanks to lactic acid bacteria.

cau_hoi: What agent causes the common cold?
giai_thich: The flu is caused by influenza viruses and other respiratory viruses, transmitted through droplets when coughing, sneezing, or by touching the nose and mouth. Viruses cannot live on their own and must invade cells to replicate. Washing hands, covering the mouth when coughing, and getting an annual flu vaccine help prevent the disease.

cau_hoi: Offspring often resemble their parents in many traits such as hair color and eye color. What is this phenomenon called?
giai_thich: Heredity is the transmission of traits from parents to offspring through genes, the "instructions" found in DNA. Each person receives half of their genes from their father and half from their mother. Due to the different combinations of genes each time, siblings can still have differences, except for identical twins who are nearly identical genetically.

cau_hoi: Which part of the cell contains genetic material and controls all cell activities?
giai_thich: The nucleus acts as the "command center", containing DNA with genes that instruct the cell to produce proteins and perform activities. The nucleus is surrounded by a nuclear membrane with many small pores for molecules to enter and exit. Mature human red blood cells do not have a nucleus, while bacterial cells do not have a true nucleus; their DNA is free in the cytoplasm.

cau_hoi: What is the role of the membrane that surrounds the outside of the cell?
D: Controls substances entering and exiting the cell
giai_thich: The cell membrane is thin, about 7-10 nanometers thick, made of two layers of lipid molecules along with many proteins. It acts like a "gatekeeper", allowing only certain substances to pass through, keeping the internal environment of the cell stable. The cell membrane also has protein "antennas" that receive signals from the outside, such as hormones.

cau_hoi: What shape does DNA have?
B: Double helix like a twisted ladder
giai_thich: The DNA molecule consists of two strands twisted around each other like a twisted ladder. The sides of the ladder are made of sugar and phosphate, while the rungs are pairs of bases A-T and G-C. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published the double helix model, partly based on X-ray images taken by Rosalind Franklin.

cau_hoi: What process is used to make traditional fish sauce in Vietnam?
D: Fermenting fish with salt, using enzymes from fish and bacteria
giai_thich: Anchovies are mixed with salt at a ratio of about 3 fish to 1 salt, and fermented in wooden barrels or jars for 12 months or more. Enzymes in the fish's intestines and salt-tolerant bacteria break down fish proteins into amino acids, creating a rich umami flavor. The high salt content prevents spoilage bacteria. Phu Quoc, Phan Thiet, and Cat Hai are famous for their traditional fish sauce.

cau_hoi: Which microorganism helps bread rise?
giai_thich: Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast consumes sugar in the dough and produces carbon dioxide. The gas is trapped in the gluten network of the flour, causing the dough to rise and creating small holes in the bread. When baked, the heat expands the gas further and then the yeast dies. The aroma of bread partly comes from the substances produced by the yeast.

cau_hoi: How many chromosomes does each cell in the human body (except for gametes and red blood cells) have?
giai_thich: There are 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 pairs; each pair consists of one from the father and one from the mother. The first 22 pairs are the same in males and females, while the 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes. Egg and sperm cells only have 23 chromosomes, so when they combine, they form a cell with a total of 46. Chimpanzees have 48 chromosomes.

cau_hoi: What is the mitochondrion referred to in the cell?
giai_thich: Mitochondria use oxygen to break down sugars and fats, producing ATP molecules that carry energy for all living activities. A heart muscle cell can contain thousands of mitochondria because it requires a lot of energy. Mitochondria have their own DNA, and we inherit mitochondria only from our mothers. Therefore, scientists use mitochondrial DNA to trace maternal lineage.

cau_hoi: What is the key difference between viruses and bacteria?
A: Viruses cannot reproduce on their own; they must invade other cells to replicate
giai_thich: Viruses are tens to hundreds of times smaller than bacteria, consisting only of genetic material wrapped in a protein coat. Outside a cell, a virus is like an inactive particle. When it invades a cell, the virus takes control, forcing the cell to produce thousands of new viruses. Therefore, many scientists debate whether viruses are considered living organisms.

cau_hoi: How do bacteria primarily reproduce?
B: Binary fission: one cell divides into two identical cells
giai_thich: Under favorable conditions, some bacteria like E. coli can divide approximately every 20 minutes. If there are no obstacles, one bacterium can produce about 1 billion bacteria in 10 hours. This is why food left out in warm weather spoils quickly and needs to be stored in the refrigerator to slow bacterial growth.

cau_hoi: Why is it necessary to keep food in the refrigerator?
A: Because food tastes better when cold
D: Low temperatures slow down the growth of bacteria and mold
giai_thich: Most bacteria that spoil food thrive best at temperatures between 5 – 60°C, known as the "danger zone." A refrigerator at about 4°C slows their reproduction significantly, while a freezer at around −18°C nearly stops it, but does not kill them. Cooking food thoroughly at high temperatures is necessary to kill most bacteria.

cau_hoi: Where are genes located in the cell?
D: On chromosomes in the cell nucleus
giai_thich: Each chromosome is a very long DNA molecule tightly coiled around proteins. A gene is a segment of DNA that carries information to produce a protein or a functional molecule. Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes. If the DNA in a human cell were stretched out, it would be about 2 meters long.

cau_hoi: What causes pickled vegetables to ferment?
B: Lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars in vegetables into lactic acid
giai_thich: When vegetables are soaked in brine, harmful bacteria find it difficult to thrive, but salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria survive. They consume sugars in the vegetables and produce lactic acid, making the pickles sour and preserving them for a long time. "Sour" pickles (moderately sour) usually take about 2 – 3 days. Korean kimchi is also made based on a similar principle.

cau_hoi: Who is known as the "father of genetics" due to his experiments with pea plants?
giai_thich: Gregor Mendel was a monk in Brno (now in the Czech Republic). From 1856 to 1863, he grew about 28,000 pea plants, observing traits such as flower color, seed color, and seed shape across generations. He discovered that traits were inherited according to mathematical laws. His work, published in 1866, was forgotten for over 30 years and was rediscovered in 1900.

cau_hoi: What pair of sex chromosomes do humans have in males?
giai_thich: Females typically have two X chromosomes (XX), while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). The Y chromosome is much smaller and carries the SRY gene that determines male sex development. The mother always passes on one X chromosome to the child, while the father can pass on either an X or a Y, so the child's sex depends on the chromosome from the father.

cau_hoi: Where do E. coli bacteria typically live?
A: In the intestines of humans and warm-blooded animals
giai_thich: Most strains of E. coli are harmless and even help produce vitamin K in the intestines. Some strains can cause food poisoning. Due to their rapid reproduction and ease of cultivation, E. coli is one of the most studied organisms, used to produce insulin and various medications. The presence of E. coli in drinking water is a sign of contamination.

cau_hoi: Why do people boil or heat water before drinking?
A: To make the water look nice
B: High temperatures kill most bacteria, viruses, and parasites
giai_thich: At 100°C, the proteins of most pathogenic microorganisms denature and they die within minutes. Boiling is a simple and effective way to ensure safe drinking water when the cleanliness of the water source is uncertain. However, boiling does not remove heavy metals or toxic chemicals from the water. In high-altitude areas, water boils at lower temperatures, so it needs to be boiled longer.

cau_hoi: What is the process called when a cell divides into two identical daughter cells for growth and replacement of old cells?
giai_thich: In mitosis, DNA is duplicated, and the chromosomes are evenly divided between the two daughter cells, with each cell having 46 chromosomes like the parent cell. Mitosis allows wounds to heal and children to grow. Meiosis is a special type of division that only produces gametes with half the number of chromosomes.

cau_hoi: How does an amoeba (a shapeshifting organism) move?
C: Extends 'pseudopodia' by flowing cytoplasm to one side
giai_thich: An amoeba is a single-celled organism with no fixed shape. It pushes cytoplasm in one direction, forming pseudopodia, and then the entire body 'flows' along. Pseudopodia are also used to engulf food such as bacteria and small algae, swallowing them into a digestive vacuole. Most amoebas are harmless, but some species living in dirty water can cause dysentery.

cau_hoi: How does the paramecium move?
D: With thousands of tiny cilia covering its body
giai_thich: The paramecium is shaped like a shoe and is about 0.1 – 0.3 mm long. Thousands of tiny cilia beat rhythmically like oars, propelling the paramecium to swim in circles in the water. The cilia also help funnel food into its 'mouth'. The paramecium has contractile vacuoles to pump excess water out, preventing it from bursting.

cau_hoi: Euglena is special because it has characteristics of both plants and animals. What is that characteristic?
A: It can photosynthesize thanks to chlorophyll, while also moving and consuming food
B: It has both bones and shells
C: It can both fly and swim
D: It has both leaves and legs
giai_thich: Euglena has chloroplasts, allowing it to photosynthesize in light, but in darkness, it can absorb organic matter from the environment. It swims using a long whip and has a red 'eye spot' to sense light and swim towards it. Organisms like this make it difficult to classify life forms strictly as 'animals' or 'plants'.

cau_hoi: Which insect transmits the malaria-causing parasite to humans through its bite?
giai_thich: The Plasmodium parasite is a single-celled organism that lives in the saliva of female Anopheles mosquitoes. When the mosquito bites, the parasite enters the bloodstream, reproduces in the liver, and then invades red blood cells. Each time the red blood cells burst, the patient experiences high fever and chills in cycles. Vietnam has significantly reduced malaria cases, aiming to eliminate the disease.

cau_hoi: In DNA, which base does A (adenine) always pair with?
giai_thich: According to the base pairing rule, A always pairs with T through two hydrogen bonds, while G pairs with X (C) through three hydrogen bonds. This allows us to deduce the sequence of one strand from the other. When DNA replicates, each strand serves as a template to create a new strand, ensuring that genetic information is accurately copied.

cau_hoi: Why are children vaccinated from a very young age?
A: So that children do not need to eat
B: To enable the immune system to early develop the ability to fight dangerous diseases
D: To help children grow taller quickly
giai_thich: Young children have an incomplete immune system and are at risk of severe complications from diseases such as measles, whooping cough, diphtheria, tetanus, and hepatitis B. Vietnam's expanded vaccination schedule began in 1985, significantly reducing these diseases. Antibodies from breast milk protect children for a short time, after which vaccines help the child's body create long-lasting immunity.

cau_hoi: What kingdom does the green mold on old bread belong to?
giai_thich: Mold grows from spores floating in the air. When they land on moist bread, the spores germinate into fungal filaments that penetrate the bread, and we only see the green or black spores on the surface. Since the fungal filaments have spread inside, cutting off the moldy part does not make the bread safe. Some molds produce toxins, so it is best to discard moldy bread or rice.

cau_hoi: Which organelle in the cell is responsible for protein synthesis?
giai_thich: Ribosomes are small "factories" that read copies of information from genes (mRNA) and link amino acids in the correct order to form proteins. A cell can have millions of ribosomes. The ribosomes of bacteria differ from those of humans, which is why many antibiotics like tetracycline target bacterial ribosomes without harming human cells.

cau_hoi: What is the function of the "Golgi apparatus" in the cell?
D: Package, sort, and send proteins to where they are needed
giai_thich: The Golgi apparatus consists of many flattened sacs stacked on top of each other like a stack of pancakes. Proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum are sent here, modified, tagged with "address labels," and packaged into small vesicles to be transported outside the cell or to other organelles. It is named after the Italian scientist Camillo Golgi, who discovered it in 1898.

cau_hoi: What is the role of lysosomes in animal cells?
C: Contain digestive enzymes to break down waste and bacteria
giai_thich: Lysosomes are small sacs containing about 50 types of enzymes that can break down proteins, fats, sugars, and DNA. They act as the cell's "clean-up and recycling" department. Inside lysosomes, the environment is acidic, so if enzymes leak out into the neutral cytoplasm, they become less active, helping to protect the cell.

cau_hoi: How do prokaryotic organisms (like bacteria) differ from eukaryotic organisms (like humans, fungi, and plants) at a fundamental level?
giai_thich: In bacteria and archaea, DNA is located in a region of the cytoplasm, not surrounded by a nuclear membrane, and there are no membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria. Eukaryotic cells are about 10 to 100 times larger than prokaryotic cells. Prokaryotic organisms appeared on Earth first, about 3.5 to 4 billion years ago.

cau_hoi: What are the common shapes of bacteria?
giai_thich: Spherical bacteria are called cocci, such as staphylococci that cause boils. Rod-shaped bacteria are called bacilli, such as bacillus anthracis and E. coli. Spiral-shaped bacteria are called spirilla. The shapes help scientists identify bacteria under a microscope. Interestingly, there are even square-shaped bacteria living in salt lakes.

cau_hoi: A trait that is expressed only when there are two identical copies of the gene (one from each parent) is called what?
giai_thich: In Mendel's pea plants, purple flowers are dominant, and white flowers are recessive. A plant will only have white flowers if it carries two white flower genes; if it has one purple flower gene, the flowers will be purple. Therefore, two purple-flowered parents can still produce white-flowered offspring if both carry the hidden recessive gene. In humans, many genetic diseases are recessive traits.

cau_hoi: In 1953, who took the famous X-ray diffraction photo "Photo 51," which helped discover the double helix structure of DNA?
giai_thich: Rosalind Franklin and her graduate student Raymond Gosling took Photo 51 at King's College London in 1952. The X-shaped image showed that DNA has a helical structure. Watson saw the photo without Franklin's knowledge. In 1962, Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins received the Nobel Prize; Franklin had passed away in 1958 from cancer at the age of 37, and the Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously.

cau_hoi: In 1996, which animal became the first mammal to be cloned from a mature cell?
giai_thich: Dolly the sheep was born at the Roslin Institute (Scotland) on July 5, 1996. Scientists took the nucleus from a mammary gland cell of a female sheep, inserted it into an egg cell that had its nucleus removed, and then stimulated the egg to develop into an embryo. Dolly was named after singer Dolly Parton. The experiment demonstrated that a mature cell still contains enough information to create an entire organism.

cau_hoi: What role do bacteria in the roots of leguminous plants play in natural cycles?
giai_thich: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air, but plants and animals cannot use it directly. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert nitrogen into ammonia; other bacteria convert ammonia into nitrates that plants absorb. When organisms die, bacteria decompose them, returning nitrogen to the soil, and some bacteria convert nitrogen back into gas. Without bacteria, this cycle would stop.

cau_hoi: How long does it take for some bacteria like E. coli to divide once under optimal conditions?
giai_thich: In the laboratory with sufficient nutrients and at 37°C, E. coli divides approximately every 20 minutes. This rate allows scientists to observe thousands of generations of bacteria in just a few years. Since 1988, scientist Richard Lenski has continuously cultured 12 strains of E. coli, tracking over 75,000 generations and observing evolution occurring before his eyes.

cau_hoi: Mendel discovered that when crossing purebred yellow pea plants with purebred green pea plants, what color are the seeds in the first generation (F1)?
giai_thich: In pea plants, the yellow seed gene is dominant over the green seed gene. Every F1 plant receives one yellow gene and one green gene, so all have yellow seeds. When F1 self-pollinates, the F2 generation has about 3 yellow seeds to 1 green seed, because the green gene that was 'hidden' in F1 appears when they meet. Mendel counted 6,022 yellow seeds and 2,001 green seeds, very close to the ratio of 3:1.

cau_hoi: How many base pairs (the 'letters' of DNA) does the human genome contain?
giai_thich: If the human genome were printed on paper, with each letter representing a base, it would require about 1,000 thick books, each with 1,000 pages. Each cell contains two copies of the genome (one from the father and one from the mother), totaling about 6 billion base pairs. Only about 1-2% of the genome consists of protein-coding genes; the rest has many regulatory roles, and some functions are still unclear.

cau_hoi: In what year was the Human Genome Project, which sequenced the entire human DNA, declared essentially complete?
giai_thich: The project started in 1990 with the collaboration of scientists from many countries, costing about $3 billion. By 2003, about 92% of the genome had been sequenced. The most difficult parts, filled with repetitive sequences, were only completed in 2022 by the 'Telomere-to-Telomere' group. Today, sequencing a human genome costs only a few hundred dollars and takes about a day.

cau_hoi: Who invented the PCR technique, which allows the amplification of a DNA segment into millions of copies in just a few hours?
giai_thich: In 1983, while driving on a mountain road in California at night, Kary Mullis came up with the idea of using repeated cycles of heating and cooling to continuously double DNA. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993. PCR is used for disease diagnosis (such as COVID-19 testing), forensic investigations, and ancient DNA research.

cau_hoi: Where is the Taq polymerase enzyme used in PCR obtained from?
C: Hot springs in Yellowstone National Park (USA)
giai_thich: In 1966, microbiologist Thomas Brock discovered the bacterium Thermus aquaticus living in hot springs at about 70°C in Yellowstone. Its DNA copying enzyme is not destroyed when heated to about 95°C in each PCR cycle. This allows PCR to run automatically without needing to add new enzyme after each cycle. This is an example of how basic research can lead to significant applications.

cau_hoi: Archaea were once mistaken for bacteria. Many species among them are famous for living in what kind of environments?
A: Extreme environments like hot springs and salt lakes
giai_thich: In 1977, scientist Carl Woese analyzed ribosomal RNA and recognized that these microorganisms are fundamentally different from bacteria, to the extent that they should be classified into a separate 'domain.' Life is divided into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Today we know that Archaea also live everywhere, including in soil, oceans, and animal intestines.

cau_hoi: What type of organism primarily produces methane gas emitted from the stomach of cows (through belching)?
giai_thich: In the rumen, microorganisms break down grass to produce hydrogen and CO₂, and then methanogenic archaea use them to produce methane gas. A cow can emit about 100 kg of methane each year, mostly through belching rather than flatulence. Methane is a greenhouse gas approximately 80 times more potent than CO₂ in the first 20 years, so scientists are experimenting with feeding cows red seaweed to reduce methane.

cau_hoi: In what year was the 'DNA fingerprinting' technique, used for identifying individuals through DNA, invented by Alec Jeffreys?
giai_thich: On September 10, 1984, at the University of Leicester (UK), Alec Jeffreys looked at X-ray film images and saw that the DNA bands of each family member of a laboratory technician were different but had some similarities. In 1986, this technique first helped exonerate a suspect and identify the real perpetrator in a case. Today, DNA testing is also used to determine biological relationships.

cau_hoi: An organism whose genome has been actively added to, removed from, or altered by humans is called what?
giai_thich: Scientists can insert genes from one species into another. For example, Bt corn carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that produces a protein toxic to stem-boring insects, helping to reduce pesticide use. GloFish are fluorescent fish that carry a glowing gene from jellyfish. The use of genetically modified organisms is strictly regulated by safety regulations in many countries.

cau_hoi: What is a gene mutation?
B: A change in the DNA sequence
D: A change in hair color due to dyeing
giai_thich: Mutations can occur randomly when DNA is copied, or due to agents such as ultraviolet rays, radiation, or certain chemicals. Most mutations have no effect, some are harmful and cause diseases, and very few are beneficial. Mutations are a source of genetic diversity, the raw material for evolution. Each person is born with about 50-100 new mutations that their parents do not have.

cau_hoi: The electron microscope, magnifying up to millions of times, was first invented in 1931 by whom?
giai_thich: Light has a wavelength too long to see objects smaller than about 0.2 micrometers. An electron beam has a much shorter wavelength, allowing the electron microscope to see viruses and even large molecules. Ernst Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986, more than 50 years after the invention. Samples must be placed in a vacuum and are often dead.

cau_hoi: In 1859, Louis Pasteur's "swan-neck flask" experiment disproved which concept?
D: Life arises spontaneously from non-living matter (like maggots from rotten meat)
giai_thich: Pasteur boiled meat broth in a flask with a long curved neck: air could enter, but dust and microorganisms were trapped in the curve. The meat broth did not spoil. When the neck was broken, microorganisms fell in, and the broth quickly became cloudy. The experiment proved that microorganisms come from other microorganisms, not spontaneously generated. Some of his original flasks remain clear to this day.

cau_hoi: In 1668, Italian scientist Francesco Redi conducted what experiment to prove that maggots do not spontaneously arise from rotten meat?
A: Covering some jars of meat with thin cloth, no maggots appeared because flies could not lay eggs
giai_thich: Redi placed meat in jars: jars left open had maggots, while jars sealed or covered with thin cloth still spoiled but had no maggots on the meat, even though flies landed on the cloth and laid eggs there. He concluded that maggots hatch from fly eggs. This is one of the earliest controlled experiments in biology.

cau_hoi: The cell theory, stating that all living organisms are composed of cells, was proposed by two German scientists in 1838-1839. Who were they?
giai_thich: Schleiden studied plants, Schwann studied animals, and they concluded that all living organisms are made up of cells. In 1855, Rudolf Virchow added an important idea: "All cells arise from pre-existing cells." The cell theory is one of the foundations of modern biology, alongside the theory of evolution and genetics.

cau_hoi: What does each triplet of bases on mRNA (called a codon) code for?
giai_thich: There are 4 types of bases, combined into triplets, resulting in 64 codons that code for 20 types of amino acids and the signals "start" and "stop." The genetic code is nearly identical in all organisms, from bacteria to humans, indicating that all life shares a common origin. In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg deciphered the first codon: UUU codes for the amino acid phenylalanine.

cau_hoi: Why is red-green color blindness more common in men than in women?
B: The gene causing the condition is on the X chromosome, and men have only one X
D: Because women do not have colored eyes
giai_thich: The condition is caused by a recessive gene located on the X chromosome. Females have two X chromosomes, so if one X carries the disease gene, the other X usually masks it. Males have only one X, so if that X carries the disease gene, they will be color blind. About 8% of males and 0.5% of females of European descent are red-green color blind. Chemist John Dalton was the first to scientifically describe this condition in himself in 1794.

cau_hoi: What significant historical role did cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) play for Earth?
C: Produced oxygen, enriching the atmosphere with oxygen about 2.4 billion years ago
giai_thich: Cyanobacteria were the first organisms to photosynthesize and release oxygen. About 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen began to accumulate in the atmosphere, known as the "Great Oxygenation Event." Oxygen caused iron to rust in the oceans, creating the red banded iron formations we see today. It also paved the way for oxygen-using organisms, such as humans, to appear later.

cau_hoi: The largest bacterium ever known, Thiomargarita magnifica, was reported in 2022. What is its approximate size?
A: The size of a soccer ball
D: About 1-2 cm long, visible to the naked eye
giai_thich: This bacterium lives on fallen mangrove leaves in the Caribbean (Guadeloupe). It has a filamentous shape like a hair, about 5,000 times larger than typical bacteria. Even more strangely, its DNA is enclosed in membrane-bound sacs, resembling the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell. This discovery changes our understanding of the size limits of bacteria.

cau_hoi: The bacterium Deinococcus radiodurans is nicknamed "Conan the Bacterium" for what ability?
A: Withstanding radiation doses thousands of times higher than lethal doses
giai_thich: Deinococcus can withstand radiation doses of about 5,000 gray, while only about 5 gray can be lethal to humans. Radiation breaks its DNA into hundreds of pieces, but the bacterium completely repairs itself within hours, thanks to multiple copies of its DNA and a special protein protection mechanism. In 2020, scientists showed it could survive for 3 years outside the International Space Station.

cau_hoi: Why do most genetically modified organisms still need to be safety tested before being released to the market?
B: To ensure safety for human health and the environment
giai_thich: Each genetically modified organism is assessed individually: does the new gene cause allergies, does it affect other organisms, does it spread to wild plants? Major scientific organizations conclude that approved genetically modified crops are safe to eat like conventional crops. However, debates about economic and environmental impacts continue.

cau_hoi: How are identical twins formed?
A: Two eggs are fertilized at the same time
D: One egg is fertilized and then splits into two separate embryos
giai_thich: Since they originate from the same zygote, identical twins have nearly identical genetic makeup and are always of the same sex. Fraternal twins result from two different eggs being fertilized at the same time, similar to regular siblings. Scientists study twins to understand which traits are determined by genes and which are influenced by the environment.

cau_hoi: What are viruses that only attack bacteria called?
giai_thich: Bacteriophages have a shape resembling a lunar lander: a "head" containing DNA and "legs" that attach to bacteria. They inject DNA into bacteria, turning them into factories that produce hundreds of new phages, then cause the bacteria to burst. Phages are the most abundant organisms on Earth, with about 10³¹ particles. Doctors are using phages to treat infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

cau_hoi: How can high temperatures during a fever affect enzymes?
A: Excessively high temperatures denature enzymes and render them inactive
giai_thich: Enzymes are proteins with a very specific three-dimensional shape, allowing them to fit perfectly with the substances they act upon, like a key in a lock. Excessively high temperatures denature proteins, causing them to lose their shape and become inactive, similar to how egg whites coagulate when boiled. This is one reason why a fever above about 41 – 42°C is very dangerous.

cau_hoi: Why do we see bubbles when we apply hydrogen peroxide to a raw potato or a wound?
A: Hydrogen peroxide is carbonated like soda
B: The enzyme catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas
giai_thich: Hydrogen peroxide is produced in cells as a harmful waste product. Most cells contain the enzyme catalase that breaks it down extremely quickly: each catalase molecule can process millions of molecules per second, making it one of the fastest enzymes known. The bubbles are oxygen. If the potato is cooked beforehand, catalase is destroyed and no bubbles will form.

cau_hoi: What process causes a snail to shrink when salt is sprinkled on it?
A: Osmosis: water from the snail's body moves out to the area with a high salt concentration
giai_thich: Osmosis is the movement of water through a membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. The salt on the snail's skin creates a very concentrated solution, pulling water out of the cells, causing the snail to lose water rapidly. Similarly, raisins soaked in water will swell, while vegetables soaked in concentrated salt water will wilt. This is why pickles are salty and vegetables become soft.

cau_hoi: What substance is the "energy currency" that all living cells use to function?
giai_thich: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) releases energy when a phosphate group is removed, providing energy for muscle contractions, nerve signal transmission, and protein synthesis. Each day, the human body produces and uses an amount of ATP nearly equal to its body weight, as each ATP molecule is recycled thousands of times. Fireflies also use ATP to produce light.

cau_hoi: What is dental plaque actually?
A: A new layer of tooth enamel
D: A biofilm consisting of millions of bacteria sticking together
giai_thich: Bacteria in the mouth adhere to teeth and secrete a sticky layer, forming a biofilm that is very difficult to remove just by rinsing. Bacteria consume sugars and excrete acids that erode tooth enamel. If not brushed away, plaque hardens into tartar. Brushing at least twice a day and using dental floss helps break down this biofilm.

cau_hoi: What usually causes Down syndrome in humans?
B: An extra chromosome 21 (three instead of two)
C: Due to a lack of nutrients
giai_thich: During the formation of egg or sperm cells, sometimes the pair of chromosome 21 fails to separate, resulting in a zygote with three chromosomes. Individuals with Down syndrome often have distinct facial features and varying degrees of developmental delay. Many live happy lives, work, and contribute to society. The syndrome is named after Dr. John Langdon Down, who described it in 1866.

cau_hoi: Where do the bacteria that cause tetanus live, making vaccination necessary for deep, dirty wounds?
A: In soil, dust, and animal feces
giai_thich: The tetanus bacteria Clostridium tetani produce very durable spores that can survive for a long time in soil. When spores enter a deep wound lacking oxygen, such as stepping on a rusty nail, they grow and release toxins that attack the nerves, causing muscle stiffness. It is the dirty soil on the nail, not the rust, that is the culprit. The tetanus vaccine is very effective and is included in children's vaccination schedules.

cau_hoi: What organisms produce gas from livestock manure in biogas pits in rural areas?
D: Anaerobic decomposing bacteria and methanogenic archaea
giai_thich: In an oxygen-free environment, microorganisms decompose pig and cow manure and organic waste, producing biogas primarily composed of methane, which is used for cooking and lighting. The remaining residue is good fertilizer for crops. Biogas pits help reduce odors, decrease water pollution, and save firewood, preventing deforestation.

cau_hoi: The gene located on the X chromosome that causes hemophilia was spread through the royal families of many European countries, originating from which queen?
giai_thich: Queen Victoria carried a hemophilia gene on one of her X chromosomes. Her son, Prince Leopold, had the disease, and two of her daughters passed the gene to the royal families of Spain and Russia. Tsarevich Alexei, son of Tsar Nicholas II, suffered from this disease. In 2009, DNA analysis of the remains of the Russian royal family confirmed this was hemophilia type B.

cau_hoi: Blood type AB in humans is an example of which type of inheritance?
C: Codominance: both A and B alleles are expressed
giai_thich: Blood type genes have three main forms: A, B, and O. Both A and B are dominant over O, but when a person has both A and B, both are expressed, resulting in blood type AB. Therefore, a type A father and a type B mother can have children with type A, B, AB, or even type O if both carry the recessive O gene.

cau_hoi: Red snapdragon flowers crossed with white snapdragon flowers produce pink offspring. What type of inheritance is this?
giai_thich: In incomplete dominance, the dominant allele does not completely overshadow the other allele, resulting in offspring with an intermediate phenotype. Red flowers have two red alleles, white flowers have two white alleles, while pink flowers have one red and one white allele, producing just enough pigment for the pink color. If two pink flower plants are crossed, the next generation will have a ratio of about 1 red: 2 pink: 1 white.

cau_hoi: Traits such as height or skin color, which are determined by many genes, are called what?
giai_thich: Each gene contributes a small part, so polygenic traits exhibit continuous variation, not divided into clear categories like Mendel's purple and white flowers. If we plot the height of many individuals, we get a bell-shaped curve. Environmental factors such as nutrition and sunlight also significantly influence these traits.

cau_hoi: Thomas Hunt Morgan won the Nobel Prize in 1933 for his genetic research on which organism?
giai_thich: In 1910, Morgan discovered a male fruit fly with white eyes instead of red. By tracking the inheritance of this trait, he demonstrated that the gene is located on a chromosome, and the white eye gene is on the X chromosome. Fruit flies are easy to breed in jars, reproduce quickly (about 10 days per generation), and have only 4 pairs of chromosomes, making them the 'stars' of the genetics lab.

cau_hoi: Calico cats (fur with three colors: orange, black, white) are almost always female. Why?
A: Because male cats only have white fur
B: The orange and black color genes are on the X chromosome, requiring two Xs to have both colors
D: Because male cats have no fur
giai_thich: In female cats, each cell randomly 'turns off' one of the two X chromosomes from the embryonic stage. If one X carries the orange gene and the other X carries the black gene, the fur patches will be orange or black depending on which X is active. Male cats only have one X, so they typically have only one of the two colors. It is very rare for male calico cats to appear, as they have two Xs and one Y (XXY).

cau_hoi: In 1869, Swiss chemist Friedrich Miescher first isolated a substance he called 'nuclein.' What do we know it as today?
giai_thich: Miescher took pus from bandages of patients in a hospital, where there were many white blood cells, and isolated a phosphorus-rich substance from the cell nucleus. At that time, no one thought this substance carried genetic information; it was believed that more complex proteins did that. It wasn't until nearly 75 years later that scientists proved DNA is the genetic material.

cau_hoi: How does RNA differ from DNA?
A: RNA has two strands, DNA has one strand
B: RNA usually has a single strand and uses the base U instead of T
C: RNA is only found in bacteria
giai_thich: RNA uses ribose sugar, while DNA uses deoxyribose (lacking one oxygen atom). In RNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine (T) and pairs with A. RNA has many roles: mRNA carries a gene copy to the ribosome, tRNA carries amino acids, and rRNA makes up the ribosome. Many scientists believe that early life may have been based on RNA, referred to as the 'RNA world.'

cau_hoi: The 'central dogma' of molecular biology, proposed by Francis Crick in 1958, describes the flow of genetic information how?
giai_thich: Information in DNA is 'transcribed' into RNA, and then RNA is 'translated' into protein. Proteins perform most of the work in the cell. Later, it was discovered that there are exceptions: some viruses like HIV can reverse transcribe from RNA to DNA using reverse transcriptase. Nevertheless, the dogma remains the basic framework for understanding how genes function.

cau_hoi: HIV belongs to which special group of viruses that can transfer genetic information from RNA to DNA?
giai_thich: HIV carries RNA and reverse transcriptase, creating a DNA copy that integrates into the genome of human immune cells. HIV attacks helper T cells, weakening the immune system. Currently, there is no vaccine, but antiviral drugs help HIV-infected individuals live healthy lives almost normally. About 8% of the human genome is remnants of ancient retroviruses that infected our ancestors.

cau_hoi: Why does the flu virus require a new vaccine almost every year?
B: The flu virus continuously mutates, changing its surface proteins, making it hard for the immune system to recognize
C: Because the old vaccine is damaged
D: Because the flu virus only appears once
giai_thich: The flu virus has RNA as its genetic material, and when it replicates, it is prone to errors, creating many small mutations that alter the surface proteins H and N. Sometimes, two different strains of the flu virus mix genes within the same cell, resulting in a completely new strain that can cause a pandemic. The names of the strains like H1N1, H5N1 are based on the types of H and N proteins.

cau_hoi: What special agent causes "mad cow disease" (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), which is neither a virus nor a bacterium?
giai_thich: Prions are misfolded proteins that can cause normal surrounding proteins to also misfold, like a chain reaction, destroying brain tissue into sponge-like holes. Prions do not have DNA or RNA and are very difficult to eliminate with heat or common chemicals. Scientist Stanley Prusiner received the Nobel Prize in 1997 for discovering prions.

cau_hoi: In 2003, scientists discovered Mimivirus, a "giant" virus. What made it surprising?
B: It is the smallest in the world
D: It is so large that it was once mistaken for a bacterium when viewed under a light microscope
giai_thich: Mimivirus was found in a cooling tower in England in 1992 and was initially thought to be a bacterium. In 2003, French scientists identified it as a virus, with a diameter of about 0.75 micrometers and a genome of nearly 1,200 genes, larger than that of some bacteria. The name "Mimi" is short for "mimicking microbe". Mimivirus infects amoebas.

cau_hoi: Why were mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria released in some places, like Nha Trang?
C: To reduce the ability of mosquitoes to transmit dengue virus
giai_thich: Wolbachia bacteria naturally live in about 60% of insect species. When introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, it hinders the development of dengue and Zika viruses within the mosquitoes. Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes reproduce and pass the bacteria to the next generation. Vietnam is one of the first countries to test this method, starting on Trí Nguyên Island (Nha Trang) in 2014.

cau_hoi: The Hawaiian bobtail squid glows thanks to bacteria. When do these bacteria glow?
B: When they are sufficiently dense, thanks to "quorum sensing" through chemical signals
giai_thich: Vibrio fischeri bacteria continuously secrete a signaling substance. When their numbers are low, the signal is diluted and they do not glow. When densely populated in the squid's light organ, the signal concentration exceeds a threshold, and they all light up together. This "quorum sensing" phenomenon allows the bacteria to coordinate as a collective. The light helps the squid erase its shadow under the moonlight.

cau_hoi: What do farmers use Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) bacteria for?
D: To make biological insecticide because it produces proteins toxic to insects
giai_thich: When ingested by insects, Bt's crystal protein is activated in the insect's alkaline gut, rupturing the gut wall, causing the insect to stop eating and die. This protein is nearly harmless to humans, birds, and fish because their guts have different environments. Bt has been used as a biological insecticide since the 1920s, and its protein-producing gene has been inserted into genetically modified corn and cotton.

cau_hoi: What dormant form allows anthrax bacteria to survive in the soil for decades?
C: Endospores – a "sleeping" form with an extremely durable shell
giai_thich: Under harsh conditions, some bacteria like Bacillus and Clostridium produce endospores within their cells, with multiple layers of shells resistant to heat, drought, chemicals, and radiation. Endospores can "sleep" for decades, even believed to be thousands of years, then "wake up" when favorable conditions arise. This is why medical instruments must be sterilized at high temperatures and pressures.

cau_hoi: The Gram staining method divides bacteria into two groups, Gram-positive and Gram-negative, based on what characteristic of the bacteria?
giai_thich: In 1884, Danish doctor Hans Christian Gram discovered that bacteria with thick cell walls stain dark purple (Gram-positive), while bacteria with thin walls and an outer membrane lose the purple color and stain pink-red (Gram-negative). Distinguishing the groups helps doctors choose appropriate antibiotics, as some antibiotics like penicillin are more effective against Gram-positive bacteria.

cau_hoi: What dangerous toxin produced by some molds growing on peanuts and damp corn can harm the liver?
giai_thich: The mold Aspergillus flavus grows on grains and stored damp peanuts, producing aflatoxin, one of the strongest liver carcinogens. Aflatoxin is not completely destroyed when cooked. Therefore, it is advisable not to eat moldy, discolored, or bitter peanuts, corn, or rice. Keeping seeds dry helps prevent mold growth.

cau_hoi: The color of traits such as eye color can be determined by genes, while the set of genes that an organism carries is called what?
giai_thich: Genotype refers to the "genetic makeup" of an individual, while phenotype refers to the expressed characteristics such as flower color, height. Two purple flower pea plants can have different genotypes: one plant carries two purple genes, while the other carries one purple gene and one recessive white gene. Phenotype is also influenced by the environment: for example, hydrangea flowers change color to blue or pink depending on soil acidity.

cau_hoi: What are different forms of the same gene (for example, the flower color gene with forms 'purple' and 'white') called?
giai_thich: Each person has two alleles for each gene, one from the father and one from the mother. If the two alleles are the same, it is called homozygous; if they are different, it is called heterozygous. Different alleles arise from slight differences in the DNA sequence, sometimes just one 'letter'. For example, the ABO blood group gene has three main alleles A, B, and O.

cau_hoi: To predict the genotype ratio in the offspring when crossing two individuals, what diagram is commonly used, named after whom?
giai_thich: British geneticist Reginald Punnett devised the square in 1905: the father's alleles are written on one side, the mother's alleles on the other, and each box represents a possible combination in the offspring. With two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa), the square gives a ratio of 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Punnett and William Bateson also discovered the phenomenon of gene linkage.

cau_hoi: In 1928, scientist Frederick Griffith conducted experiments with pneumonia-causing bacteria on mice and discovered what?
C: Harmless bacteria can 'transform' into disease-causing bacteria when mixed with dead pathogenic bacteria
giai_thich: Griffith injected mice with a mixture of live harmless bacteria and heat-killed pathogenic bacteria. The mice died, and live pathogenic bacteria were found in their blood. A 'transforming factor' was transferred from the dead bacteria to the live bacteria. In 1944, Oswald Avery and colleagues proved that this factor was DNA.

cau_hoi: In 1952, the experiment by Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase using radioactive-labeled bacteriophages confirmed what?
D: DNA, not protein, is the genetic material
giai_thich: Hershey and Chase labeled the DNA of the phage with radioactive phosphorus and the protein coat with radioactive sulfur. After the phage infected the bacteria, they used a blender to separate the phage coat from the bacteria. Radioactive phosphorus was found inside the bacteria, while sulfur remained outside, indicating that only DNA entered to produce new viruses. Hershey received the Nobel Prize in 1969.

cau_hoi: According to 'Chargaff's rule', in the DNA of all species, the amount of base A is always equal to which base?
giai_thich: In 1950, biochemist Erwin Chargaff measured the DNA composition of many species and found that A is always equal to T, and G is always equal to C, although the ratio of A + T to G + C varies among species. This rule was an important clue that helped Watson and Crick realize how bases pair in the double helix.

cau_hoi: How many bacteria can fit in a teaspoon of fertile garden soil?
giai_thich: Soil is one of the most densely populated environments on Earth: one gram of soil can contain billions of bacteria from thousands of species, along with kilometers of fungal threads. They decompose fallen leaves and dead organisms, returning nutrients to plants. The characteristic 'earthy' smell after rain is largely due to the geosmin produced by Streptomyces bacteria. Many important antibiotics have been discovered from soil bacteria.

cau_hoi: Dengue fever, common in Vietnam during the rainy season, is caused by which agent?
C: Dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes
giai_thich: The Dengue virus has 4 different serotypes. A person infected with one serotype may experience more severe illness if infected with another serotype later. The disease causes high fever, muscle pain, and can lead to a decrease in platelets causing bleeding. Aspirin should not be taken without medical advice when dengue fever is suspected as it increases the risk of bleeding. Prevention mainly involves mosquito and larva control.

cau_hoi: Why do doctors advise taking antibiotics at the prescribed dose, even when feeling better?
B: To kill all bacteria, preventing surviving ones from becoming drug-resistant
C: To avoid having to go back for a check-up
giai_thich: When starting to take a few doses, the weakest bacteria are killed first, so one feels better, but the stronger ones remain. If the medication is stopped early, they can multiply again and gradually become drug-resistant. However, new guidelines show that for some diseases, shorter treatment courses can still be effective, so the most important thing is to follow the doctor's instructions.

cau_hoi: What is the yolk of an ostrich egg (not fertilized) commonly considered in biology?
D: One of the largest single cells
giai_thich: The yolk of an unfertilized bird egg is essentially a giant egg cell filled with stored nutrients, surrounded by layers of egg white and shell. Therefore, the yolk of an ostrich egg is considered one of the largest cells in the animal kingdom. In humans, the egg cell is the largest cell, with a diameter of about 0.1 mm, nearly large enough to be seen with the naked eye.

cau_hoi: What components do plant cells have that animal cells typically do not?
A: Cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts, and large vacuoles
giai_thich: The rigid cell wall helps plants stand upright, chloroplasts aid in photosynthesis, and large vacuoles store water, making the cell turgid. Animal cells do not have cell walls, making them more flexible and varied in shape. Both have nuclei, mitochondria, ribosomes, and cell membranes. Fungal cells have cell walls but are made of chitin and do not have chloroplasts.

cau_hoi: In 1958, Meselson and Stahl's experiment was called "the most beautiful experiment in biology." What did it prove?
D: DNA doubles in a semi-conservative manner: each daughter DNA consists of one old strand and one new strand
giai_thich: Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria in a medium containing heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), then switched to light nitrogen (¹⁴N). They centrifuged the DNA and found that after one generation, the DNA had an intermediate mass, as predicted if each daughter molecule retained one old strand. The simple and clear experiment definitively answered the question, earning it praise as very beautiful.

cau_hoi: Scientist Barbara McClintock won the Nobel Prize in 1983 for discovering what while studying corn?
B: "Jumping genes" – segments of DNA that can move positions within the genome
giai_thich: In the 1940s and 1950s, McClintock observed corn kernels with unusual colored spots and realized that some DNA segments "jumped" from one place to another, turning on or off color-producing genes. Initially, many scientists did not believe her. More than 30 years later, when jumping genes were found in bacteria and many other organisms, she was finally recognized. Today we know that nearly half of the human genome is the remnants of jumping genes.

cau_hoi: "Epigenetics" studies what?
C: Changes that turn genes on or off without altering the DNA sequence
giai_thich: Chemical "marks" such as methyl groups attached to DNA or to proteins that coil DNA can make genes easier to read or lock them down. Every cell in the body has the same DNA, but thanks to these marks, skin cells differ from nerve cells. The environment and diet can influence epigenetic marks. In honeybees, larvae fed royal jelly become queen bees due to epigenetic changes.

cau_hoi: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother. Scientists use it to trace the "Mitochondrial Eve." What is that?
A: The woman who is the common maternal ancestor of all living people today
giai_thich: In 1987, analysis of mitochondrial DNA from many ethnic groups showed that all living people today share a common maternal ancestor who lived in Africa about 150,000 to 200,000 years ago. She was not the only woman at that time; other women were also our ancestors, but their mitochondrial lines have since died out. Similarly, there is "Y-chromosomal Adam" through the paternal line.

cau_hoi: How do cancer cells differ from normal cells in a significant way?
D: They divide uncontrollably and do not undergo programmed cell death
giai_thich: Normal cells have "brakes" and "accelerators" that control division and self-destruct when severely damaged (programmed cell death). When many mutations accumulate and damage these systems, cells divide chaotically, forming tumors and potentially spreading elsewhere. Smoking and ultraviolet radiation are mutagenic agents that can lead to cancer.

cau_hoi: What is the benefit of "programmed cell death" (apoptosis) for the body?
C: Removes damaged, old, or excess cells neatly
giai_thich: Every day, an adult human body has about 50 to 70 billion cells that undergo programmed cell death, replaced by new cells. In embryos, apoptosis helps form fingers: the cells in the membrane between the fingers die off. If this mechanism fails, faulty cells can survive and become cancerous. Ducks retain webbing because the cells there do not undergo apoptosis.

cau_hoi: In meiosis, the phenomenon where chromosomes from the father and mother exchange segments with each other is called what?
giai_thich: Before forming egg or sperm cells, homologous chromosome pairs align closely and "swap" corresponding segments. This way, each gamete carries a new combination of genes never seen before. Along with the random distribution of chromosomes, crossing over helps each child (except identical twins) inherit a unique genetic combination.

cau_hoi: Why can't cells keep growing indefinitely and must divide?
A: As a cell grows, the surface area increases more slowly than the volume, making it difficult to exchange enough materials
C: Because the cell membrane would burst immediately
D: Because cells are afraid of getting big
giai_thich: When a cube doubles in size, the surface area increases 4 times but the volume increases 8 times. Cells take in nutrients and expel waste through their surface, so an oversized cell will not have enough "doors" to serve the interior. Therefore, large organisms are made up of many small cells rather than one giant cell.

cau_hoi: How does the sodium-potassium pump on the nerve cell membrane, which helped Jens Skou win the Nobel Prize in 1997, work?
C: Uses ATP energy to pump sodium out and potassium into the cell, against the concentration gradient
giai_thich: This is an example of active transport: substances are moved against the concentration gradient, requiring energy expenditure. Each time one ATP is used, the pump pushes 3 sodium ions out and brings 2 potassium ions in, creating an electrical gradient across the membrane, the basis of nerve impulses. The brain uses a large portion of its energy just to operate these pumps.

cau_hoi: Which chemist proposed the "lock and key" model describing how enzymes work in 1894?
giai_thich: Emil Fischer suggested that enzymes have an active site shaped to fit the substrate like a lock fits a key, so each enzyme typically acts on a specific type of substance. Later, the model was refined to the "induced fit": the enzyme slightly changes shape when the substrate binds, like a glove fitting a hand. Fischer won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1902.

cau_hoi: Most enzymes in the human body work best at what temperature?
giai_thich: Enzymes in the body have evolved to function best at body temperature. When it's too cold, reactions slow down; when it's too hot, enzymes become denatured. Each enzyme also has its own optimal pH: pepsin in the stomach works best in acidic conditions, while enzymes in the small intestine require a slightly alkaline environment. Enzymes from hot spring bacteria work well at 70 – 80°C.

cau_hoi: In cells, the system of protein fibers that helps maintain cell shape and acts as a "railway" for transporting substances is called what?
giai_thich: The cytoskeleton consists of microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments, functioning like a skeleton and a railway system. Motor proteins like kinesin walk along microtubules, pulling cargo vesicles to where they are needed, similar to pedestrians. During cell division, microtubules form the mitotic spindle that pulls chromosomes apart.

cau_hoi: How is cholera bacteria primarily transmitted?
B: Contaminated drinking water and food infected with human feces
giai_thich: The cholera bacterium Vibrio cholerae releases a toxin that causes the intestines to expel massive amounts of water, leading to severe dehydration where patients can lose up to tens of liters of water daily, posing a rapid life-threatening risk. Treatment primarily involves rehydration and electrolyte replacement, such as with oral rehydration solutions, considered one of the most significant medical advances of the 20th century. Using clean water and safe sanitation is the best prevention method.

cau_hoi: Why do cut potatoes and apples turn brown when exposed to air?
A: Enzymes in the cells break down upon contact with oxygen, producing brown pigments
B: Because they are immediately infected by mold
D: Because they are burned by sunlight
giai_thich: When a knife cuts through cells, the enzyme polyphenol oxidase encounters phenolic compounds and oxygen in the air, resulting in brown pigments similar to melanin. Soaking apples in lemon juice (acid weakens the enzyme) or diluted salt water helps slow browning. Conversely, this reaction creates the desired brown color for black tea and ripe dates.

cau_hoi: Fermented foods like yogurt, pickles, and kimchi contain "probiotics." How are probiotics beneficial?
giai_thich: Probiotics are beneficial live microorganisms, such as certain strains of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. They compete with harmful bacteria and help maintain a balanced gut microbiome, especially after antibiotic use. However, each strain has different effects, and not all products marketed as "probiotics" have proven efficacy.

cau_hoi: The process of composting organic waste from kitchen scraps and leaves is primarily carried out by whom?
D: Bacteria, fungi, and small soil organisms like worms
giai_thich: Microorganisms decompose organic matter, generating heat: a large compost pile can reach temperatures of about 55 – 70°C, enough to kill many weed seeds and pathogens. After a few months, the waste transforms into dark, nutrient-rich humus for plants. Composting helps reduce landfill waste, where organic waste decomposes anaerobically, producing methane, a greenhouse gas.

cau_hoi: Mary Mallon, a cook in New York in the early 20th century, is famously known as "Typhoid Mary" for what reason?
A: She carried the typhoid bacteria without symptoms, infecting many people
C: She was a doctor treating typhoid
giai_thich: Mary Mallon was the first person in the U.S. identified as an "asymptomatic carrier" of typhoid fever. She was healthy but the bacteria lived in her gallbladder, and through the meals she prepared, at least 51 people became infected. She did not believe she was causing illness and was isolated for a total of about 26 years. Her story highlights the importance of handwashing when preparing food.

cau_hoi: The plague pandemic known as the "Black Death" was transmitted from rats to humans primarily through what?
B: Bites from fleas living on rats
giai_thich: Fleas that suck blood from infected rats carry the bacteria, which multiply and block the flea's intestines. The hungry flea bites humans and vomits the bacteria into the bite. When the disease spreads to the lungs, it can also be transmitted directly through droplets. Today, the plague is rare and treatable with antibiotics if detected early. The bacterium is named after Alexandre Yersin.

cau_hoi: "The immune system" of bacteria against viruses is the source of which famous gene-editing tool?
giai_thich: Bacteria store snippets of DNA from viruses that have attacked them in repetitive segments called CRISPR, like a "blacklist." When a virus returns, the bacteria produce guide RNA according to the blacklist, bringing the Cas9 enzyme to cut the viral DNA. Scientists have adapted this mechanism into a "molecular scissors" that can cut DNA at any chosen location. The first CRISPR segments were discovered by Japanese scientist Yoshizumi Ishino in 1987.

cau_hoi: The SARS-CoV-2 virus that causes COVID-19 attaches to human cells via which part on its surface?
giai_thich: The spike protein on the virus's surface binds to the ACE2 receptor on the respiratory cell surface like a key opening a door. These spikes create a "crown" shape when viewed under an electron microscope, hence the virus is called "corona" (crown). Most COVID-19 vaccines train the immune system to recognize the spike protein.

cau_hoi: Why should we use sunscreen and avoid intense sunlight at noon?
A: Ultraviolet rays can cause DNA mutations in skin cells, increasing the risk of skin cancer
C: Because sunlight makes hair grow longer
D: Because sunlight changes the color of the eyes
giai_thich: Ultraviolet B rays cause adjacent T bases on DNA to stick together, leading to errors when the cell replicates DNA. Cells have repair mechanisms, but if damage is too extensive, mutations accumulate. Sunburn in childhood increases the risk of skin cancer later. Melanin in the skin is a natural sunscreen, but additional protection is needed during intense sunlight.

cau_hoi: In addition to the main chromosomes, many bacteria also have small circular DNAs that can exchange with each other. What are they called?
giai_thich: Plasmids often carry "extra" genes such as antibiotic resistance genes. Bacteria can transfer plasmids to each other, even between different species, facilitating the rapid spread of drug resistance genes. Scientists use plasmids as "vehicles" to introduce desired genes into bacteria, such as the human insulin gene into E. coli.

cau_hoi: Rotavirus is the leading cause of what illness in young children, and can be prevented by an oral vaccine?
giai_thich: Rotavirus spreads through the fecal-oral route, easily transmitting among young children, causing vomiting and diarrhea, which can lead to severe dehydration. Most children have been infected with rotavirus by age 5 if not vaccinated. Vietnam has been producing an oral rotavirus vaccine (Rotavin-M1) since 2012. Rehydration with oral rehydration solutions is the most important treatment.

cau_hoi: What process do yeast use to produce alcohol from sugar in the absence of oxygen?
giai_thich: In the absence of oxygen, yeast breaks down sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide to obtain energy, but only yields less energy compared to when oxygen is present. This is the process used to make beer, wine, and rice wine. When the alcohol concentration reaches about 12-15%, yeast usually dies from the alcohol it produces.

cau_hoi: What is the general equation for cellular respiration?
C: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
giai_thich: Cellular respiration is almost the reverse process of photosynthesis: glucose is "burned" slowly and controlled by enzymes to release energy into ATP, rather than combusting like burning paper. The carbon dioxide we exhale is the product of this process in trillions of cells. About 40% of the energy from glucose is retained, while the rest is converted to heat to help keep the body warm.

cau_hoi: What special shape do human red blood cells have that helps them carry oxygen efficiently and pass through capillaries?
giai_thich: The biconcave disc shape increases the surface area for gas exchange and helps oxygen diffuse quickly inside. Red blood cells are very flexible and can bend to pass through narrower capillaries than themselves. Red blood cells have a diameter of about 7-8 micrometers. In sickle cell disease, red blood cells are rigid and crescent-shaped, easily causing blockages.

cau_hoi: When culturing bacteria on agar plates, a visible cluster of bacteria that develops from an initial single cell is called what?
giai_thich: Each colony consists of millions of identical bacteria arising from a single original bacterium. The shape, color, and surface of the colony help microbiologists identify the species. Counting the number of colonies indicates how many viable bacteria were in the original sample. The agar plate culturing technique was developed by Robert Koch's group, and the plate is named after his assistant, Julius Petri.

cau_hoi: The endoplasmic reticulum in cells has two types, rough and smooth. What "particles" are found on the surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
giai_thich: Ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum produce proteins that will be sent outside the cell or embedded in membranes, such as digestive enzymes and hormones. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes, synthesizes fats, and helps detoxify; liver cells have a lot of smooth endoplasmic reticulum. The endoplasmic reticulum is a system of folded membranes connected to the nuclear membrane.

cau_hoi: What inheritance pattern does albinism (very white skin and hair, light-sensitive eyes) follow?
A: Recessive gene: requires receiving the disease gene from both parents
D: Dominant gene: only one gene needed
giai_thich: Albino individuals lack the enzyme that produces melanin due to carrying two copies of the recessive gene. Parents may be completely normal but carry a hidden disease gene, so each time they have a child, there is about a 1 in 4 chance the child will be albino. Albino individuals need to protect their skin and eyes very carefully from sunlight. Albinism occurs in animals as well, such as snakes, tigers, and crocodiles.

cau_hoi: What is the phenomenon called when bacteria transfer genes directly to other bacteria (not through reproduction)?
giai_thich: In most organisms, genes are transmitted "vertically" from parents to offspring. Bacteria also exchange genes "horizontally" in three ways: conjugation (connecting cytoplasmic bridges and transferring plasmids), transformation (picking up free DNA), and transduction (via bacteriophages). This allows antibiotic resistance genes to spread rapidly among different bacterial species in hospitals.

cau_hoi: During conjugation, bacteria transfer DNA to each other through which structure?
D: A thin connecting tube called a sex pilus
giai_thich: Bacteria "give" a thin tube that attaches to the "recipient" bacteria, pulling the two cells closer together, and then transferring a plasmid copy through the bridge. In 1946, Joshua Lederberg and Edward Tatum discovered this phenomenon in E. coli; Lederberg won the Nobel Prize in 1958 at the age of 33. Conjugation helps bacteria share survival "tips" with each other.

cau_hoi: What is the characteristic shape of the rabies virus when viewed under an electron microscope?
giai_thich: The rabies virus belongs to the Rhabdovirus family, with "rhabdo" meaning "rod" in Greek, having a round end and a flat end like a bullet. After entering the body through a bite, the virus travels along the nerves to the brain at a slow rate, a few mm to a few cm each day. Therefore, getting vaccinated immediately after being bitten is still timely to create immunity before the virus reaches the brain.

cau_hoi: Scientists estimate that viruses in the ocean kill approximately what percentage of marine microorganisms each day?
giai_thich: Each liter of seawater contains billions of viruses, mostly bacteriophages that infect bacteria and algae. When cells are broken by viruses, organic matter and nutrients are released back into the water, nourishing other microorganisms. This "viral loop" significantly impacts the carbon cycle and global climate, even though we cannot see it.

cau_hoi: The genetic code of most genes starts with which codon, also coding for the amino acid methionine?
giai_thich: The codon AUG acts like the "capital letter at the beginning of a sentence," signaling the ribosome to start translation. Therefore, most newly synthesized proteins begin with methionine, although it is often removed later. The three codons UAA, UAG, and UGA are "punctuation marks" signaling the end. Since there are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, many amino acids are encoded by multiple different codons.

cau_hoi: Huntington's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder, is an example of a genetic disease caused by a dominant gene. What does this mean?
B: Requires two copies of the gene
D: Only one copy of the disease gene from either parent is needed to develop the disease
giai_thich: If one parent carries the Huntington gene, each child has about a 50% chance of inheriting the disease gene. The disease gene has a segment of three "letters" CAG that is repeated too many times. The disease usually appears in middle age. In 1993, scientists identified this gene by studying several large families living by Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela.

cau_hoi: The ability to roll one's tongue into a U-shape was once taught as a simple Mendelian trait. What did later studies show?
B: Completely due to a dominant gene
C: Not that simple: even identical twins may have one who can roll and one who cannot
giai_thich: In 1940, geneticist Alfred Sturtevant proposed that tongue rolling was due to a dominant gene, and it was included in textbooks for many years. But just a few years later, studies on identical twins showed inconsistent results, and many people learned to roll their tongues as they grew up. Sturtevant himself later acknowledged this. This is an example of how science continually corrects itself.

cau_hoi: How did eukaryotic cells' nuclei appear in the history of life compared to bacteria?
B: Appeared at the same time as Earth
D: Appeared much later, about 1.6 – 2 billion years ago
giai_thich: For the first 1.5 – 2 billion years, life on Earth consisted only of prokaryotic organisms like bacteria and archaea. The oldest fossil of eukaryotic cells is about 1.6 – 1.8 billion years old. Eukaryotic organisms likely arose when one ancient bacterium "swallowed" another bacterium, which later became the mitochondrion.

cau_hoi: Why are antibiotic-resistant bacteria called "superbugs"?
A: Because they resist many types of antibiotics, making them hard to treat
giai_thich: Bacteria like MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) resist many common antibiotics, causing hard-to-treat infections in hospitals. Antibiotic resistance is estimated to be related to millions of deaths each year worldwide. Scientists are searching for new antibiotics, including using artificial intelligence, such as the antibiotic halicin discovered in 2020. Using antibiotics correctly is how everyone can help prevent this.

cau_hoi: What is the main reason that most viral diseases are harder to treat with drugs than bacterial diseases?
A: Because viruses live outside the body
B: Viruses replicate inside our cells, using the cell's own machinery
C: Because viruses do not have DNA or RNA
giai_thich: Antibiotics target parts that only bacteria have. Viruses use the ribosomes and enzymes of human cells, making it very difficult to find antiviral drugs that do not harm the cells. Antiviral drugs often target specific enzymes of the virus, such as HIV drugs or Tamiflu for influenza. Therefore, vaccines are the most important "weapon" against many viral diseases.

cau_hoi: How do dengue fever and malaria differ in terms of their causative agents?
B: Dengue fever is caused by worms, malaria by viruses
C: Dengue fever is caused by viruses, malaria by single-celled parasites
giai_thich: Both diseases are transmitted by mosquitoes but different species and different agents. The Dengue virus is much smaller than the Plasmodium parasite, which is a complete eukaryotic cell. Therefore, malaria drugs like artemisinin do not work on dengue fever. Aedes mosquitoes usually bite during the day, while Anopheles mosquitoes bite at night.

cau_hoi: The cell membrane allows water to pass through very quickly thanks to special protein channels. What are they called?
giai_thich: In 1992, Peter Agre discovered aquaporin on the red blood cell membrane, the "water pipes" that allow billions of water molecules to pass through each second while blocking ions. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003. The kidneys use aquaporin to reabsorb water; when the body is dehydrated, hormones cause the kidneys to add more aquaporin to retain water.

cau_hoi: The soil bacterium Streptomyces is the source of many types of antibiotics. What was the first antibiotic that cured tuberculosis, discovered in 1943?
giai_thich: In 1943, graduate student Albert Schatz in Selman Waksman's laboratory in the U.S. isolated streptomycin from the bacterium Streptomyces griseus. This was the first antibiotic effective against tuberculosis bacteria. Waksman received the Nobel Prize in 1952 and was also the one who coined the term "antibiotic." Today, about two-thirds of natural antibiotics are derived from this group of bacteria.

cau_hoi: In humans, what is special about chromosome number 1 and chromosome number 21?
A: Number 1 is the largest, number 21 is one of the smallest chromosomes
C: Both are only found in males
giai_thich: Chromosomes are numbered by size from largest to smallest. Chromosome 1 contains about 249 million base pairs with approximately 2,000 genes. Initially, it was thought that number 22 was the smallest, but later it was found that chromosome 21 is actually smaller. Because it is small and contains fewer genes, having an extra chromosome 21 (Down syndrome) can still allow for survival, while having extra larger chromosomes usually does not.

cau_hoi: In vitro fertilization helped the world's first baby, Louise Brown, to be born in which year?
giai_thich: Louise Brown was born on July 25, 1978, in England thanks to doctors Patrick Steptoe and scientist Robert Edwards. Robert Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010. To date, over 12 million babies worldwide have been born using this technique. In 1998, the first three babies in Vietnam were born through in vitro fertilization at Tu Du Hospital (Ho Chi Minh City).

cau_hoi: Phenylketonuria (PKU) can be detected early by which test in newborns?
B: Taking a few drops of blood from the heel for newborn screening
giai_thich: Children with PKU lack the enzyme that breaks down the amino acid phenylalanine; if untreated, it accumulates and causes brain damage. In 1960, Robert Guthrie developed a test using a drop of blood on filter paper. If detected early, the child can follow a special diet that limits phenylalanine and develop normally. Today, heel prick blood tests screen for many different congenital diseases.

cau_hoi: The type of earwax, whether dry or wet, is determined by a single gene. Dry earwax is common in which community?
giai_thich: The ABCC11 gene has a variant that causes dry earwax, a gray flaky type, and less smelly sweat. This variant is very common in East Asian people such as Koreans, Chinese, and Japanese, while most African and European people have wet, brownish-yellow earwax. This is one of the few traits in humans that is clearly determined by a single gene in a Mendelian fashion.

cau_hoi: Some people feel that cilantro tastes like soap. According to research, what is this related to?
A: A gene variant of the olfactory receptor (OR6A2) sensitive to aldehydes in cilantro
B: Due to eating too much sugar
giai_thich: Cilantro contains aldehyde compounds, which are also found in soap and some insects. In 2012, a study involving tens of thousands of people found a gene variant near the olfactory receptor gene OR6A2 associated with the perception of cilantro tasting like soap. The proportion of people who dislike cilantro varies among communities, being lower in places where cilantro is commonly consumed.

cau_hoi: How do neurons differ from most other cells in terms of their ability to divide?
C: Most mature neurons no longer divide
giai_thich: Most neurons in the brain are formed before birth and exist nearly for a lifetime. Therefore, brain and spinal cord injuries are often difficult to recover from. In contrast, skin, intestinal, and blood cells are continuously renewed. However, the brain can still form new connections between neurons throughout life and can generate a few new neurons in certain areas.

cau_hoi: In animal cells, which structure helps organize the mitotic spindle when the cell divides?
giai_thich: The centrosome consists of two centrioles arranged at right angles to each other, located near the nucleus. Before division, the centrosome duplicates, and the two centrosomes move to opposite poles of the cell and emit microtubules that form the mitotic spindle to pull the chromosomes. Plant cells do not have centrioles but can still form a mitotic spindle. Centrioles are also the base of cilia and flagella in many cells.

cau_hoi: Why are genetically modified organisms created faster and more accurately than traditional breeding?
A: Because they do not need cells
B: Can insert exactly one desired gene instead of mixing thousands of genes through breeding
C: Because they are made by machines
D: Because they do not need genes
giai_thich: Traditional breeding mixes the entire genome of two parents and then must select through many generations to retain good traits and eliminate bad traits. Genetic technology can insert a specific gene, even from another species. Today, tools like CRISPR also allow precise editing of existing genes without adding foreign genes.

cau_hoi: What is the basic unit that packages DNA in the nucleus, consisting of DNA wrapped around a protein core, called?
giai_thich: DNA wraps around a core made of 8 histone protein molecules, forming "beads" strung on the DNA strand. These beads coil and fold in multiple layers, allowing a 2 m long DNA strand to fit within a nucleus just a few thousandths of a millimeter wide. Chemical marks on histones can tighten (turn off genes) or loosen (turn on genes) the DNA.

cau_hoi: Why do viruses need a "host" to survive long-term?
D: Because viruses cannot generate energy or proteins on their own and must use the host cell's machinery
