giai_thich: Outside of cells, viruses do not eat, breathe, or grow; they are just inactive particles that can be destroyed by sunlight, heat, and soap. Each type of virus typically infects only certain host species, as it requires a "key" that fits the receptor on the cell. When a virus "jumps" to a new species, such as from animals to humans, it can cause new outbreaks.

cau_hoi: Monkeypox, rabies, and avian influenza are examples of what type of disease?
C: Diseases transmitted from animals to humans
giai_thich: About 60% of known infectious diseases in humans and around 75% of emerging diseases originate from animals. Deforestation, wildlife trade, and intensive farming increase the chances for pathogens to "jump" to humans. Therefore, scientists advocate for a "One Health" approach, considering human, animal, and environmental health interconnected.

cau_hoi: In 1917, microbiologist Félix d'Hérelle discovered and named which type of virus that was later used to treat infections?
giai_thich: D'Hérelle worked at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, observing "clear zones" on cultured bacteria where the bacteria were destroyed by an invisible agent. He named it "bacteriophage" (bacteria eater) and used it to treat dysentery. When penicillin was discovered, phage therapy was forgotten in the West but continued to be used in Georgia and Russia. Today, phages are being researched again to combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

cau_hoi: What is special about Mycoplasma bacteria compared to most other bacteria?
A: Size of a grain of rice
B: Lack a cell wall and are among the smallest living cells
giai_thich: Mycoplasma only has a soft cell membrane and no rigid cell wall, so antibiotics like penicillin, which attack cell walls, are ineffective against them. Some species are only about 0.1 – 0.3 thousandths of a millimeter in size, with very small genomes. They are subjects of study to understand the "minimal genome" necessary for life.

cau_hoi: Why do jams with a lot of sugar and salted fish last a long time without spoiling?
A: Because sugar and salt are antibiotics
B: Because sugar and salt make food frozen
C: Because bacteria fear the color white
D: High concentrations of sugar and salt draw water out of bacterial and mold cells, preventing their growth
giai_thich: This is an application of osmosis: microorganisms in an overly salty or sweet environment will lose water, shrink, and stop reproducing. Honey also rarely spoils because it is too sweet, low in water, and slightly acidic. Archaeologists have found thousands-year-old honey in Egyptian tombs that is still edible.

cau_hoi: "Pasteurization" of milk is what?
A: Boiling milk for a long time
B: Heating milk at moderate temperatures for a short time to kill pathogenic microorganisms while preserving flavor
giai_thich: Initially, Louis Pasteur devised a method of gently heating wine to prevent it from souring. Today, milk is typically heated to about 72°C for 15 seconds and then rapidly cooled, killing most pathogenic bacteria such as bovine tuberculosis bacteria. UHT sterilized milk is heated to about 135 – 140°C for a few seconds, allowing it to last for months outside the refrigerator when unopened.

cau_hoi: Which organelle in the cell breaks down toxic substances like hydrogen peroxide and some fats?
giai_thich: Peroxisomes are small bags containing enzymes like catalase. In liver and kidney cells, peroxisomes help detoxify alcohol and break down long-chain fatty acids. Some rare genetic diseases are caused by malfunctioning peroxisomes, such as the disease in the film "Lorenzo's Oil." In plants, peroxisomes participate in the metabolism of fats in germinating seeds.

cau_hoi: In 2016, Japanese scientists discovered the bacterium Ideonella sakaiensis at a recycling site that has what ability?
D: Consume and break down PET plastic used for water bottles
giai_thich: The bacterium secretes two enzymes that cut PET plastic into small molecules that it uses as food. Scientists have improved this enzyme to break down plastic much faster. However, the best solution remains to reduce plastic use and recycle properly, as bacterial degradation is still slow compared to the massive amount of plastic waste.

cau_hoi: What is the famous white chalk cliff at Dover (England) primarily made of?
C: The limestone shells of trillions of tiny plankton (coccolithophores) that accumulated under the ancient sea
giai_thich: About 70 – 100 million years ago, this area was the warm seabed. Tiny plankton like coccolithophores have shells made of tiny limestone discs, which, when they die, sink and accumulate into thick layers of chalk hundreds of meters thick. Traditional chalkboard chalk is also made from this type of rock. Today, coccolithophores still bloom in the sea, visible from satellites as turquoise streaks.

cau_hoi: African sleeping sickness is caused by the single-celled parasite Trypanosoma, transmitted through the bite of which insect species?
giai_thich: The tsetse fly feeds on the blood of humans and animals in tropical Africa. The Trypanosoma parasite resembles a small snake with a flagellum, living in the blood and then invading the brain, causing sleep disturbances and confusion. The parasite continuously changes its surface protein 'coat' to evade the immune system, making it very difficult to create a vaccine. Thanks to control programs, the number of cases has decreased by more than 95% since 2000.

cau_hoi: Green fluorescent protein (GFP) from jellyfish, which helped three scientists win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2008, is used in research how?
C: Attached to other proteins to 'tag' them, allowing them to be seen glowing green in living cells
giai_thich: In 1962, Osamu Shimomura isolated GFP from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria, needing to collect about 10,000 jellyfish each summer. Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien later successfully transformed GFP into a tagging tool and created many other colors. Thanks to GFP, scientists can observe cancer cells spreading or nerve cells developing in living organisms.

cau_hoi: In 2020, the artificial intelligence AlphaFold made headlines by solving which problem in biology, helping the authors win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024?
A: Accurately predicting the three-dimensional shape of proteins from amino acid sequences
giai_thich: The shape of a protein determines its function, but determining the shape experimentally can take years. DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts shapes quickly and accurately, nearly as well as experiments, and has published predicted structures for over 200 million proteins. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper share the 2024 Nobel Prize with David Baker, who designed entirely new proteins.

cau_hoi: Chimpanzees have 48 chromosomes, while humans have 46. How do scientists explain this difference?
B: Two chromosomes from the ancestor fused into chromosome 2 in humans
giai_thich: Human chromosome 2 looks like two chimpanzee chromosomes fused together. The strongest evidence is that there are remnants of a telomere (which only exists at the ends) in the middle of chromosome 2 and a second centromere that has become inactive. This discovery is clear evidence of a common ancestor between humans and great apes.

chu_de: "Stop codons" in the genetic code are which codons that signal the ribosome to end the protein chain?
giai_thich: When the ribosome encounters one of the three stop codons, there is no tRNA carrying the corresponding amino acid, and a special protein causes the protein chain to be released. Scientists have given them fun nicknames: 'amber', 'ochre', and 'opal'. Mutating a normal codon into a stop codon often results in a short, non-functional protein.

cau_hoi: In 2018, Chinese scientists successfully cloned which animal for the first time using the method similar to that of Dolly the sheep?
giai_thich: The two long-tailed macaques were named Zhong Zhong and Hua Hua, combined to form 'Zhong Hua'. Scientists experimented with hundreds of embryos to obtain two living monkeys. Cloning primates helps create genetically identical animals for disease research, but also raises many ethical debates. Previously, in 2005, South Korea successfully cloned the first dog named Snuppy.

cau_hoi: What special ability do 'magnetotactic' bacteria have?
D: Create small magnetic crystal chains in cells, helping them swim along the Earth's magnetic field lines
giai_thich: In 1975, microbiologist Richard Blakemore observed some bacteria in mud always swimming toward the north pole of a magnet. They contain magnetite crystals arranged in chains like tiny compasses. In the Northern Hemisphere, the magnetic field lines slope downwards, helping bacteria swim down into the mud where they prefer low oxygen. Scientists study them for magnetic materials and targeted drugs.

cau_hoi: What is the characteristic of the human Y chromosome compared to the X chromosome?
B: Much smaller, containing only about a few dozen protein-coding genes
giai_thich: The X chromosome has about 800-900 protein-coding genes, while Y has only about 50-70 genes. Scientists believe that X and Y were once a matching pair about 200-300 million years ago, then Y gradually lost genes due to not recombining with X. In 2023, the human Y chromosome was sequenced completely for the first time from end to end.

cau_hoi: The protozoan Toxoplasma gondii is famous for what strange behavior in infected mice?
D: Mice lose their fear of cat odor, making them easy prey for cats, helping the parasite return to its main host, the cat
giai_thich: Toxoplasma only reproduces sexually in the intestines of cats. In infected mice, experiments show that they become less fearful and even attracted to the smell of cat urine, making them more likely to be eaten, helping the parasite complete its life cycle. Humans can also become infected with Toxoplasma through undercooked meat or cat feces, so it is important to wash hands after cleaning the litter box.

cau_hoi: What principle do the techniques of 'cell culture' and 'cultured meat' in the laboratory rely on?
C: Cultivating animal cells to proliferate in a nutrient environment outside the body
giai_thich: Scientists take a small amount of muscle cells from animals and grow them in a tank with nutrients so they divide into tissue masses. In 2013, the first cultured meat burger was cooked and tasted in London, costing about 250,000 euros. In 2020, Singapore was the first country to allow the sale of cultured chicken meat. This technology hopes to reduce the need for livestock farming, but the cost is still high.

cau_hoi: What is the function of cilia on the surface of respiratory cells?
A: Continuously beat to push mucus containing dust and bacteria up to the throat
giai_thich: Each respiratory cell has about 200 – 300 cilia, beating about 10 – 20 times per second in a wave-like motion, pushing mucus up to the throat for swallowing or coughing out. Cigarette smoke paralyzes the cilia, causing smokers to cough to expel phlegm. Cilia are also found in the fallopian tubes and in the brain.

cau_hoi: What is the purpose of cell banks, seed banks, and DNA banks?
B: To preserve valuable genetic resources for future research and conservation
giai_thich: Seeds, cells, and DNA are stored at very low temperatures, such as liquid nitrogen at around −196°C, which can keep them viable for decades to hundreds of years. The "Frozen Zoo" in San Diego (USA) preserves cells from over 1,000 species, many of which are critically endangered. In 2020, scientists cloned a black-footed ferret from cells frozen since 1988.

cau_hoi: What is the role of the 'SRY' gene on the Y chromosome?
D: Activates male development in the embryo
giai_thich: Around the 6th to 7th week of pregnancy, the SRY gene activates a series of other genes, causing the embryo to develop as male. Without SRY, the embryo develops as female. The SRY gene was discovered in 1990. In many other species, sex is determined in very different ways: for example, by the temperature of egg incubation in turtles, or the number of chromosomes in bees.

cau_hoi: What disease did the first human gene therapy in 1990 treat for 4-year-old Ashanti DeSilva?
C: Severe combined immunodeficiency due to ADA enzyme deficiency
giai_thich: Ashanti lacked the ADA enzyme, so her immune system was nearly non-functional, making her susceptible to dangerous infections. Doctors took her white blood cells, used a modified virus to insert the correct ADA gene, and then infused them back into her body. The therapy helped her become healthier, although she still needed additional medication. This was a milestone paving the way for modern gene therapy.

cau_hoi: What does the 'fluid mosaic model' of the cell membrane, proposed in 1972 by Singer and Nicolson, suggest about the cell membrane?
A: Like a 'sea' of fluid lipids in which proteins float like rafts
C: Is as rigid as a brick wall
D: Consists of a layer of metal
giai_thich: The cell membrane is not static; lipid molecules and many proteins can move laterally quite freely, like icebergs floating on the sea. This fluidity allows the membrane to self-heal when small punctures occur, enabling the cell to change shape and fuse membranes when transporting substances. Cholesterol in the membrane helps maintain its fluidity, preventing it from becoming too fluid when hot and too rigid when cold.

cau_hoi: What notable evolutionary event was recorded in a 2019 experiment selecting E. coli bacteria that began in 1988?
B: A strain of bacteria evolved the ability to consume citrate in the presence of oxygen, something E. coli typically cannot do
giai_thich: In Richard Lenski's experiment, around generation 31,500 (in 2003), one of the 12 E. coli strains suddenly gained the ability to use citrate, a substance available in the growth medium, as food in the presence of oxygen. Analysis of periodically frozen samples showed that this ability required a series of mutations to occur sequentially. Detailed studies on this event have been published over many years, including in 2012 and later.

cau_hoi: In what year was the smallest and most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth, Prochlorococcus, discovered?
giai_thich: Prochlorococcus is so small that it previously slipped through sampling nets and was only discovered in 1988 using a laser cell counter. Each milliliter of tropical seawater can contain about 100,000 cells. It is estimated that there are about 3 × 10²⁷ Prochlorococcus cells in the ocean, producing a significant portion of the oxygen we breathe.

cau_hoi: Why are scientists interested in the tiny hydra species?
A: It seems to not age due to stem cells continuously renewing its body
giai_thich: The hydra is about 1 cm long, living in freshwater ponds, and is a relative of jellyfish. Its body is continuously renewed by stem cells, to the extent that scientists have observed it for many years without seeing signs of aging. If cut into many pieces, each piece can grow into a new hydra. The name "hydra" comes from the multi-headed serpent in Greek mythology that regrows its heads when cut off.

cau_hoi: Planaria is famous for its regeneration ability. What did 19th-century experiments show?
A: The flatworm only regrows its tail
B: The flatworm transforms into a fish
D: A small piece as small as 1/279 of the body can still grow into a complete flatworm
giai_thich: In 1898, geneticist Thomas Hunt Morgan cut a flatworm and found that a very small piece, about 1/279 of the body, could still regenerate into a new flatworm. The secret lies in the pluripotent stem cells called neoblasts scattered throughout the body. Planaria also has simple 'eyes' and a small brain, and some controversial experiments suggest that the flatworm that grows a new head can still 'remember' what it has learned.

cau_hoi: What is the correct order of the main phases in mitosis?
giai_thich: In prophase, chromosomes condense and the mitotic spindle forms. In metaphase, chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and are pulled to opposite poles. In telophase, the nuclear membrane re-forms and the cytoplasm divides. Students in many countries remember this order using the English acronym 'PMAT'.

cau_hoi: How many daughter cells does a cell produce through meiosis, and how many chromosomes does each daughter cell have compared to the original cell?
A: 2 cells, with the full number of chromosomes
C: 4 cells, double the number of chromosomes
D: 4 cells, each with half the number of chromosomes
giai_thich: Meiosis consists of two successive divisions, but DNA only replicates once, resulting in 4 cells from one cell with 46 chromosomes, each having 23. Thus, when the egg and sperm combine, the chromosome number returns to 46. In females, meiosis produces only 1 large egg and several small polar bodies that degenerate.

cau_hoi: What is the term for a complete photograph of all the chromosomes of a cell, arranged in pairs and by size?
giai_thich: To create a karyotype, scientists culture cells, halt them at metaphase when the chromosomes are most condensed, stain them, and take photographs. Karyotypes help detect chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome or broken and translocated chromosome segments. It wasn't until 1956 that scientists accurately determined that humans have 46 chromosomes; previously, many believed there were 48.

cau_hoi: How does the sickle cell disease occur due to a small change in the gene?
A: Due to a virus inserting into the gene
C: Only one 'letter' (base) is changed, altering one amino acid in hemoglobin
giai_thich: In the beta hemoglobin gene, the codon GAG (coding for glutamic acid) changes to GTG (coding for valine) at position 6. This single change causes hemoglobin molecules to stick together into fibers when oxygen is low, deforming red blood cells into a sickle shape. In 1949, Linus Pauling referred to this as the first 'molecular disease' when he demonstrated that the hemoglobin of affected individuals differs from normal hemoglobin.

cau_hoi: How do diploid and haploid cells differ?
A: Diploid has two sets of chromosomes, haploid has only one set
B: Diploid has one set, haploid has two sets
giai_thich: Most human body cells are diploid (2n = 46), with one set from the father and one from the mother. Egg and sperm cells are haploid (n = 23). In some organisms, such as male bees or many moss species, the adult body is haploid. In plants, polyploidy (multiple sets) is quite common and often results in larger, healthier plants.

cau_hoi: In 1975, César Milstein and Georges Köhler created 'monoclonal antibodies' by fusing antibody-producing cells with which type of cell?
D: Cancerous myeloma cells (which live indefinitely in culture)
giai_thich: B lymphocytes produce antibodies but do not live long outside the body. Fusing with myeloma cells creates 'hybridoma' cells that both produce a single type of antibody and divide indefinitely. Monoclonal antibodies are now used in pregnancy tests, rapid tests, and many cancer and autoimmune drugs. The two scientists received the Nobel Prize in 1984 and did not patent their discovery.

cau_hoi: The lactic acid bacteria used to make yogurt, Lactobacillus bulgaricus, is named after which country, where a medical student discovered it in 1905?
giai_thich: Bulgarian student Stamen Grigorov studied yogurt from his homeland and discovered this bacterium in Geneva in 1905. Scientist Élie Metchnikoff later suggested that Bulgarian farmers lived longer partly due to their consumption of yogurt, contributing to yogurt's fame across Europe. Today, the scientific name of this species is Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus.

cau_hoi: Viroids, the smallest known disease-causing agents, differ from viruses in what way?
B: Are just a naked circular RNA, without a protein coat
giai_thich: In 1971, scientist Theodor Diener discovered that the pathogen causing potato spindle disease was a circular RNA molecule about 360 bases long, which does not encode any proteins. Viroids primarily cause diseases in plants such as tomatoes, coconuts, and citrus. The 'cadang-cadang' disease caused by viroids has killed tens of millions of coconut trees in the Philippines. Some scientists consider viroids to be 'living fossils' of the ancient RNA world.

cau_hoi: In 1959, Max Perutz determined the three-dimensional structure of which protein after more than 20 years of research using X-rays?
giai_thich: Perutz began studying hemoglobin in 1937 and took 22 years to solve its structure, which consists of 4 protein chains, each with a heme group containing iron. Colleague John Kendrew solved the structure of myoglobin in muscle. The two shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1962, the same year Watson, Crick, and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in Physiology.

cau_hoi: In 2010, the J. Craig Venter Institute announced the 'Synthia' cell. What is special about this cell?
A: It is a living bacterial cell with a genome entirely synthesized by humans
B: It is the first cloned human cell
C: It is a cell without DNA
D: It is a cell from Mars
giai_thich: Scientists chemically synthesized the entire genome of about 1.08 million base pairs of the bacterium Mycoplasma mycoides and then implanted it into a cell of another Mycoplasma species that had its DNA removed. The cell 'rebooted' and lived, reproducing according to the new genome. They even encoded some 'watermarks' in the genome, such as an email address and a quote from physicist Richard Feynman.

cau_hoi: In 2013, French scientists announced Pandoravirus, a giant virus larger than Mimivirus. What was surprising about its genome?
B: Most of its genes do not resemble any known genes
D: It is identical to the human genome
giai_thich: Pandoravirus was found in sediments off the coast of Chile and in a water pond in Australia, measuring about one thousandth of a millimeter, with a genome of about 2.5 million base pairs, much larger than many bacteria. About 90% of its genes do not resemble any genes in the database, opening a mysterious 'Pandora's box'. Giant viruses have led scientists to debate the boundaries between viruses and life.

cau_hoi: The bacterium Alcanivorax borkumensis is famous for helping to address which environmental issue?
D: Oil spills in the ocean, as it consumes hydrocarbons in oil
giai_thich: Normally, Alcanivorax is very sparse in seawater, but when there is an oil spill, they proliferate rapidly and become the dominant bacteria, breaking down hydrocarbons into CO₂ and water. After the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico in 2010, oil-eating microorganisms decomposed a significant portion of the oil and gas. Scientists added nutrients to promote this process.

cau_hoi: "Hayflick limit" discovered in 1961 indicates what about normal human cells?
C: They can only divide about 40 – 60 times in culture before stopping
giai_thich: Leonard Hayflick discovered that normal cells in culture divide a certain number of times before aging and stopping division, contrary to the previous belief that cultured cells could live forever. It was later understood that the main reason is the shortening of telomeres after each division. Cancer cells like HeLa surpass this limit.

cau_hoi: In 2016, in Mexico, a baby was born using the "mitochondrial replacement" technique, sometimes referred to by the media as the "baby with three parents." What is the purpose of this technique?
A: To avoid transmitting genetic diseases caused by defective mitochondria from mother to child
giai_thich: The mother carried a severe neurological disease due to mutated mitochondrial DNA. Doctors transferred the nucleus from the mother's egg into a donor egg that had its nucleus removed but contained healthy mitochondria. The baby carries nuclear DNA from both parents and a very small amount of mitochondrial DNA (only 37 genes) from the donor. In 2015, the UK was the first country to legally allow this technique.

cau_hoi: In 1953, the great chemist Linus Pauling proposed what model of DNA before Watson and Crick?
D: A triple helix with phosphate groups inside – a false model
giai_thich: In early 1953, Pauling, who had discovered the alpha helix structure of proteins, published a model of triple-stranded DNA. Watson and Crick immediately recognized the chemical flaws in this model because negatively charged phosphate groups could not be close together in the center. This prompted them to race and find the correct model a few weeks later. Pauling still received two Nobel Prizes in his lifetime: Chemistry in 1954 and Peace in 1962.

cau_hoi: Restriction enzymes, tools for cutting DNA at specific sequences (Nobel 1978), originate from where?
B: Bacteria used to cut DNA of invading viruses
giai_thich: Bacteria have enzymes that recognize a short sequence, such as GAATTC, and cut DNA there, helping to destroy the DNA of bacteriophages. They mark their own DNA with a methyl group to avoid self-cutting. Werner Arber, Daniel Nathans, and Hamilton Smith received the Nobel Prize in 1978. Restriction enzymes act like "molecular scissors," paving the way for genetic engineering.

cau_hoi: In 1973, how did Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer create the first genetically modified organism?
C: Cutting and splicing genes into a plasmid and then introducing it into E. coli bacteria
giai_thich: They used restriction enzymes to cut an antibiotic resistance gene and a plasmid, then used ligase to splice them together into "recombinant DNA," and introduced it into E. coli. The bacteria carried and passed on the new gene to subsequent generations. Boyer later co-founded Genentech in 1976, a pioneering biotechnology company producing human insulin from bacteria.

cau_hoi: What do scientists call the protein p53 due to its anti-cancer role?
giai_thich: When DNA is damaged, p53 accumulates and halts the cell cycle for repair, or if the damage is too severe, it instructs the cell to undergo apoptosis. The TP53 gene is mutated in about half of human cancer cases. In 1993, Science magazine named p53 "Molecule of the Year." Individuals with inherited p53 mutations have a very high risk of cancer.

cau_hoi: The archaeon "Strain 121," discovered in 2003 near hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor, holds what record?
B: Able to live and multiply at 121°C, the temperature commonly used to sterilize medical instruments
giai_thich: At the deep ocean floor, high pressure keeps water from boiling even at temperatures above 100°C. Strain 121 can double at 121°C and survive for 2 hours at 130°C. Sterilization autoclaves in hospitals typically use 121°C, so the bacterium was named after this number to emphasize its extraordinary resilience. Such organisms are called extremophiles.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon of "bioluminescent sea" glowing blue when waves crash at night on many beaches, including in Vietnam, is usually caused by which organism?
giai_thich: When disturbed by waves or swimmers, single-celled dinoflagellates emit flashes of blue light due to a luciferin-luciferase reaction. The light can startle predators or attract larger predators to eat the ones feeding on the dinoflagellates. While beautiful, dense blooms of these algae can deplete oxygen in the water and harm marine life.

cau_hoi: William Ratcliff's "snowflake yeast" experiment in 2012 showed what about the origin of multicellular organisms?
D: Single-celled yeast can evolve into multicellular forms in just a few weeks of selection
giai_thich: Scientists placed yeast in a test tube, allowed it to settle for a few minutes, and then only kept the sediment to continue culturing. After about 60 days, clusters of snowflake yeast appeared: the daughter cells did not separate from the mother cell, and the heavier clusters sank faster. Some cells in the cluster even died to allow the cluster to split and reproduce. The experiment suggests that multicellularity can evolve quite easily.

cau_hoi: Which two scientists published the structure of DNA in the journal Nature in 1953 in an article of approximately how many words?
giai_thich: The article by Watson and Crick on April 25, 1953, was only about 900 words long, accompanied by a drawing of the double helix by Odile Crick, Francis's wife. The most famous line in the article is: "We have observed that the specific pairing we had postulated immediately suggests a possible mechanism for the replication of genetic material." The same issue contains an article by Franklin and Wilkins providing experimental evidence.

cau_hoi: Why is the information in DNA copied so accurately that there is only about one error in a billion bases?
B: The replicating enzyme self-checks for errors, along with DNA repair systems
C: Because DNA is made of metal
giai_thich: The enzyme DNA polymerase mostly chooses the correct base most of the time and has the ability to backtrack and remove incorrectly attached bases. Then, mismatch repair systems check again. Three scientists, Tomas Lindahl, Paul Modrich, and Aziz Sancar, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2015 for their research on DNA repair mechanisms.

cau_hoi: "Halophilic" organisms like some archaea Halobacterium can survive in which environment?
A: Salt lakes and salt flats with nearly saturated salt concentrations
giai_thich: Halophilic archaea maintain very high potassium ion concentrations inside their cells to balance with the salty environment outside, preventing dehydration. Many species have reddish pigments like bacteriorhodopsin, which use light to generate energy. Therefore, salt evaporation ponds and some salt lakes often appear pink when viewed from an airplane.

cau_hoi: Which type of human cell can live the longest, nearly throughout a person's life?
C: Neurons in the cortex and lens cells of the eye
giai_thich: Research using radioactive carbon from nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s shows that most cortical neurons have a lifespan equal to that of the individual. The proteins in the eye's lens are also formed before birth and last a lifetime. In contrast, intestinal lining cells live only about 3-5 days, while red blood cells last about 120 days.

cau_hoi: Every day, how many small damages does the DNA in a human cell endure that need to be repaired?
giai_thich: DNA is continuously damaged by heat, reactive oxygen molecules produced during cellular metabolism, ultraviolet rays, and chemicals. Estimates suggest that each cell may need to repair about 10,000 to 100,000 damages each day. The repair systems work tirelessly; when they fail, mutations accumulate rapidly, increasing the risk of cancer.

cau_hoi: Why do researchers often use mice in biomedical experiments?
A: Because mice are exactly like humans
C: Mice have many genes similar to humans, reproduce quickly, are easy to care for, and can be genetically modified
D: Because mice do not get sick
giai_thich: About 85% of the protein-coding genes in mice have corresponding genes in humans. Mice reproduce quickly, with each generation taking about 10 weeks, and scientists can create "knockout" mice to study the role of individual genes. In 2007, the Nobel Prize was awarded for the method of creating genetically modified mice. Current ethical regulations require reducing the number of animals, improving experiments, and replacing them with alternative methods when possible.

cau_hoi: What role do viruses that "eat" bacteria and other cells in the ocean play in the carbon cycle?
D: Releasing organic matter from broken cells, helping to recycle nutrients in the water
giai_thich: When viruses break down bacterial and algal cells, organic matter is released into the seawater, feeding other bacteria instead of moving up the food chain to fish. This phenomenon, called the "viral loop," retains a large portion of carbon and nutrients in the surface water. Some organic matter sinks to the ocean floor, contributing to long-term carbon storage.

cau_hoi: What significance do "acid-loving" organisms living in the Rio Tinto River (Spain), with red water and a pH of about 2, have for space scientists?
A: This environment resembles some regions that may exist on ancient Mars
B: This is a rocket launch site
C: The river water comes from the Moon
D: This is where extraterrestrial life is found
giai_thich: The Rio Tinto River flows through a region rich in iron and sulfur mined for thousands of years, with water as acidic as lemon juice. Nevertheless, many bacteria, archaea, algae, and fungi still thrive here, deriving energy from iron and sulfur. NASA and European scientists use Rio Tinto to test life detection equipment for Mars, where there was once iron-rich water.

cau_hoi: Why do scientists use the roundworm C. elegans in research, helping many people win Nobel Prizes?
A: Its body is transparent, has only about 1,000 cells, and the fate of each cell has been mapped
C: Because it has a human brain
D: Because it is as big as a snake
giai_thich: The C. elegans worm is about 1 mm long, and the adult hermaphrodite has exactly 959 body cells. John Sulston tracked the origin of each cell from the egg through a microscope. Research on this worm has led to Nobel Prizes for programmed cell death (2002), RNA interference (2006), and GFP (2008). In 1998, it was the first multicellular organism to have its entire genome sequenced.

cau_hoi: In 1998, what important achievement did scientist James Thomson (USA) accomplish in stem cell research?
C: Successfully culturing human embryonic stem cells in the laboratory
giai_thich: Embryonic stem cells can become any type of cell in the body. Culturing them opened up hopes for curing many diseases, but also raised ethical controversies because human embryos must be used. In 2007, Thomson and Shinya Yamanaka simultaneously published methods to convert mature human skin cells into stem cells, helping to avoid many of these controversies.

cau_hoi: According to estimates in 2018, how does the total carbon mass of all bacteria on Earth compare to that of all animals?
B: Animals are 100 times more than bacteria
D: Bacteria are about 35 times more than animals
giai_thich: Yinon Bar-On's research group estimated the biomass on Earth to be about 550 billion tons of carbon: plants account for about 450 billion tons, bacteria about 70 billion tons, while all animals only about 2 billion tons. Humans account for about 0.06 billion tons but have reduced plant biomass by about half since agriculture began. Most bacteria live deep underground.

cau_hoi: "DNA barcoding" is used by scientists for what purpose?
B: Identifying species based on a short characteristic gene segment
giai_thich: Similar to barcodes on goods, a short gene segment like the mitochondrial COI gene differs among animal species but is the same within a species. This method helps identify species from small samples like fish scales, bird feathers, detect seafood mislabeled by species, or discover new species. In 2003, scientist Paul Hebert (Canada) proposed this method.

cau_hoi: In 2020, what method did Vietnamese and international scientists use to confirm that the Hoan Kiem turtle (Rafetus leloii) still lives in Dong Mo Lake (Hanoi)?
A: Analyzing environmental DNA (eDNA) in lake water samples and capturing a specimen
giai_thich: Organisms continuously leave DNA in the environment through shedding skin, mucus, and waste. Filtering lake water and analyzing DNA helps detect species living there without needing to see them. The eDNA results from Dong Mo Lake, along with capturing a specimen for sampling in 2020, confirmed it was a Rafetus leloii, bringing hope for this critically endangered turtle species.

cau_hoi: In 2016, Professor Tom Patterson (USA) was infected with bacteria resistant to all antibiotics and fell into a coma. What therapy saved him?
C: Injecting specially selected phages to kill the bacteria
giai_thich: During a trip to Egypt, Patterson was infected with the super antibiotic-resistant bacterium Acinetobacter baumannii. His wife, an epidemiologist, contacted scientists across the United States to find phages that could kill this strain of bacteria. After being injected with a phage mixture, he regained consciousness and recovered. The story drew the world's attention back to phage therapy.

cau_hoi: When DNA replicates, one strand is synthesized continuously, while the other is synthesized in short segments. What are these short segments called?
giai_thich: The enzyme DNA polymerase can only extend the strand in one direction. Since the two DNA strands run in opposite directions, one strand is synthesized continuously along the replication fork, while the other must be synthesized in short segments of about 100-200 bases in humans, which are then joined together. These segments are named after the Japanese scientists Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki, who discovered them in 1968.

cau_hoi: In addition to the 20 common amino acids, what is the name of the 21st amino acid that contains the element selenium and is encoded by a codon that is normally a stop codon?
giai_thich: Selenocysteine is incorporated into proteins when the UGA codon, which is normally a stop signal, is accompanied by a special structure on mRNA. Humans have about 25 proteins containing selenocysteine, many of which are antioxidant enzymes. Therefore, selenium is an essential micronutrient in the diet, found in fish, eggs, and nuts. Some archaea even use the 22nd amino acid, pyrrolysine.

cau_hoi: In 2016, the J. Craig Venter Institute created a bacterium with a minimal genome, called JCVI-syn3.0. How many genes does this genome have?
giai_thich: Scientists sequentially removed genes from the Mycoplasma bacterium to find the minimum number of genes required for a cell to survive and reproduce. The result was 473 genes. Surprisingly, about 149 of those genes have unknown functions, indicating that we still do not fully understand what is necessary for life, even in the simplest cells.

cau_hoi: "LUCA" is the term scientists use to refer to what?
B: The last common ancestor of all living organisms today
giai_thich: LUCA (Last Universal Common Ancestor) is not the first organism, but rather a population of organisms from which all bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes today are descendants. Analysis of the common genes of all life suggests that LUCA may have lived about 4 billion years ago, likely in a hot environment similar to hydrothermal vents. A 2024 study estimates LUCA lived about 4.2 billion years ago.

cau_hoi: What impact did Erwin Schrödinger's book "What is Life?" (1944) have?
A: Suggested that genes are a "non-repeating crystal" containing information codes, inspiring Watson and Crick
giai_thich: Schrödinger, one of the founders of quantum mechanics, wondered how hereditary material could be stable over many generations and contain so much information. He suggested it was a molecule with a non-repeating structure, like a code. Both James Watson and Francis Crick have stated that this small book motivated them to shift their focus to genetic research.

cau_hoi: In 1961, what did Francis Crick and Sydney Brenner's experiment with viruses demonstrate about the genetic code?
A: The genetic code is read in sets of five
C: The genetic code is read in sets of three consecutive bases, non-overlapping
D: The genetic code is read one base at a time
giai_thich: They created mutations by adding or removing bases in the gene of a bacteriophage. Adding or removing 1 or 2 bases disrupted the gene, but adding or removing exactly 3 bases usually allowed the gene to function. This shows that the code is read in a "frame" of three from a fixed starting point, similar to reading a sentence made up of three-letter words: shifting one letter will render the entire sentence meaningless.

cau_hoi: In 1975, scientists met at Asilomar (California) to do what?
A: Discuss and establish safety rules for recombinant DNA experiments
giai_thich: When gene editing techniques first emerged, scientists were concerned about the risks of creating dangerous bacteria. About 140 scientists, lawyers, and journalists met and provided guidelines on laboratory safety levels. The Asilomar conference became an example of the scientific community self-regulating new technology, which is echoed in discussions about CRISPR and artificial intelligence.

cau_hoi: The "Philadelphia chromosome", discovered in 1960, is related to which disease and led to which famous drug?
giai_thich: Scientists in Philadelphia (USA) discovered an unusual short chromosome in the cells of patients with chronic myeloid leukemia. It was later found to be caused by a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, creating the BCR-ABL fusion gene that activates continuous cell division. The drug imatinib, developed in 2001, specifically inhibits this protein, turning a once-fatal disease into a manageable condition.

cau_hoi: Elephants have very few cases of cancer despite their massive bodies with trillions of cells. What was discovered in 2015 as a reason?
A: Elephants eat a lot of grass
C: Elephants have about 20 copies of the "guardian gene" p53, while humans only have 1 pair
giai_thich: Theoretically, the larger the animal, the more cells divide, and the higher the risk of cancer. However, elephants and whales do not have a higher incidence of cancer than humans, known as the "Peto's paradox". In 2015, scientists discovered that elephants have about 20 copies of the p53 gene, making cells with DNA damage more likely to undergo apoptosis. This is a new research direction for cancer prevention in humans.

cau_hoi: Bdelloid rotifers, tiny creatures living in freshwater, are famous in biology for what?
D: Existing for tens of millions of years consisting only of females, reproducing asexually, and "borrowing" many genes from other organisms
giai_thich: No one has ever found a male bdelloid rotifer. They reproduce through unfertilized eggs for tens of millions of years. Strangely, about 8-10% of their genes come from bacteria, fungi, and plants through horizontal gene transfer. They can withstand complete desiccation, and in 2021, scientists "revived" rotifers frozen in Siberian permafrost for about 24,000 years.

cau_hoi: In 2016, scientists discovered that tardigrades have a special protein called Dsup. What effect does this protein have when introduced into cultured human cells?
D: Reduces about 40% of DNA damage from X-rays
giai_thich: Dsup (Damage suppressor) binds to DNA like a shield, protecting it from free radicals generated by radiation. When Japanese scientists introduced the Dsup gene into human cells, the cells experienced significantly less DNA damage when exposed to X-rays. This discovery could help protect astronauts from cosmic radiation in the future.

cau_hoi: What ability does the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae on plant leaves have related to weather?
A: Helps water freeze at higher than normal temperatures, potentially affecting snow and rain
giai_thich: Proteins on the surface of Pseudomonas syringae act as "nuclei" for ice crystals to form at around −2°C, while pure water can remain liquid down to about −40°C before freezing. This helps the bacteria damage leaves to obtain nutrients. Bacteria carried by the wind into clouds can help create snow and rain. Ski resorts even use its protein to make artificial snow.

cau_hoi: The nematocysts of jellyfish and sea anemones hold what record?
C: Firing stingers with an acceleration of about 5 million times gravity, one of the fastest processes in biology
giai_thich: Each nematocyst contains a capsule with a tightly coiled stinger under very high pressure, about 150 times atmospheric pressure. When touched, the capsule opens and the stinger is fired in less than a millionth of a second, strong enough to penetrate the hard shell of small crustaceans. Each nematocyst can only be used once, after which it is replaced.

cau_hoi: In 1907, zoologist Henry Wilson conducted what famous experiment with sponges?
B: Pressing sponges through mesh fabric to separate them into individual cells, which then reassemble into a new sponge
giai_thich: Sponges are among the simplest multicellular animals, lacking organs, nerves, or muscles. When separated, the cells crawl back together, recognize like cells, and rearrange into a functioning organism. The experiment helped study how cells "recognize" and adhere to each other, a crucial step in the emergence of multicellular organisms.

cau_hoi: Volvox algae is an interesting example of what in biology?
D: A sphere made up of thousands of cooperating cells, near the boundary between unicellular and multicellular
giai_thich: Volvox are tiny green spheres in water, each consisting of about 500 to 60,000 flagellated cells, connected by cytoplasmic bridges and beating their flagella together to roll the sphere. Most cells do not reproduce; only a few specialized cells produce small daughter spheres inside. The cells in Volvox have begun to specialize, representing the early stages of true multicellular organisms.

cau_hoi: Paramecium and other ciliates have what special feature regarding their cell nucleus?
C: Have two types of nuclei: one large nucleus controlling daily activities and one small nucleus used for reproduction
giai_thich: The large nucleus contains many copies of genes needed frequently, like a "quick reference library". The small nucleus holds the original genome and is only used when two paramecia exchange genetic material through conjugation. After conjugation, the old large nucleus is destroyed and recreated from the new small nucleus. Some ciliates even "translate" genetic codes slightly differently than usual.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2001 was awarded to Leland Hartwell, Tim Hunt, and Paul Nurse for discovering what?
A: Molecules that control the cell cycle, such as cyclin and CDK
giai_thich: Hartwell used baker's yeast, Nurse used fission yeast, to find genes that control the cell's progression through each stage. Tim Hunt discovered cyclin protein in sea urchin eggs, with concentrations rising and falling in a cyclical manner like a clock. Cyclin activates the enzyme CDK, like a key turning on a machine. These "brakes" and "accelerators" malfunctioning are a cause of cancer.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 was awarded to three scientists, including Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, for determining the structure of which organelle?
giai_thich: Ribosomes consist of hundreds of thousands of atoms, making it extremely difficult to determine their structure. Ada Yonath started in the 1980s with the idea of crystallizing ribosomes, which many considered impossible. The ribosome structure shows that it is RNA, not protein, that performs the amino acid linking reaction, supporting the idea of an "RNA world." It also aids in designing new antibiotics targeting bacterial ribosomes.

cau_hoi: In 1969, female scientist Dorothy Hodgkin determined the three-dimensional structure of which hormone after 34 years of research?
giai_thich: Hodgkin used X-ray diffraction, having previously determined the structure of penicillin (1945) and vitamin B12 (1956), for which she received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964, becoming the third woman to receive this award. She began researching insulin in 1935 and finally solved it in 1969, when computers were powerful enough. She worked while suffering from severe arthritis in her hands.

cau_hoi: In 1991, Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann received the Nobel Prize for the "patch clamp" technique. What does this technique allow?
D: Measure current through a single ion channel on a cell membrane
giai_thich: They pressed a super-thin glass pipette against the cell membrane, creating a sealed patch that contained only a few ion channels. This allowed them to measure extremely small currents, on the order of a few trillionths of an ampere, when a single channel opened and closed. The technique helps understand how nerve, heart, and muscle cells work, and how many types of drugs affect them.

cau_hoi: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1995 was awarded for the discovery of genes that control embryonic development in fruit flies, such as genes determining where legs and wings grow. What is this famous group of genes called?
giai_thich: Mutations in Hox genes can cause fruit flies to grow legs where antennae should be, or to have an extra pair of wings. Surprisingly, Hox genes are very similar in flies, mice, and humans, arranged on chromosomes in the exact order of body parts from head to tail. Edward Lewis, Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard, and Eric Wieschaus received the prize for these discoveries.

cau_hoi: Why are zebrafish widely used in biological research?
A: Transparent embryos that develop outside the mother's body, allowing observation of each organ forming
B: Because they are as large as whales
giai_thich: Zebrafish are small striped fish originating from South Asia. The eggs hatch after about 3 days, and within the first 24 hours, the heartbeat can be seen under a microscope. Zebrafish also have the ability to regenerate damaged hearts, retinas, and fins. About 70% of human genes have corresponding genes in zebrafish, making them useful for studying many diseases.

cau_hoi: Craig Venter and the Celera company participated in the "race" to sequence the human genome with a public project using which method?
B: Whole genome "shotgun" sequencing: cutting DNA into many small pieces and then using computers to assemble them
giai_thich: Instead of reading each mapped region sequentially, Celera cut the entire DNA into millions of random pieces, read each piece, and then used supercomputers to find overlapping sections to assemble them like a puzzle. In 2000, both groups announced drafts of the human genome at the White House. The genome that Celera sequenced was largely Venter's own.

cau_hoi: In 1967, biologist Lynn Margulis proposed the endosymbiotic theory, suggesting that mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from where?
A: From free-living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells and lived symbiotically
giai_thich: Margulis's paper was rejected by about 15 journals before being published. She pointed out that mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA, ribosomes similar to bacteria, double membranes, and divide like bacteria. In the 1970s and 1980s, genetic analysis confirmed that mitochondria are closely related to a group of alpha-proteobacteria, while chloroplasts are closely related to cyanobacteria. Today, this is one of the major ideas in biology.

cau_hoi: In 2008, scientists discovered "Sputnik", a special type of virus for what reason?
A: It is a virus without genetic material
C: It is a virus from space
D: It is a "virus of viruses": it can only replicate by parasitizing a giant virus infecting an amoeba
giai_thich: Sputnik was found in a cooling tower in Paris, replicating using the machinery of the giant Mamavirus when both infected an amoeba. Sputnik causes the giant virus to replicate less efficiently, acting as a parasite of a parasite, hence it is called a "virophage" (virus eater). This discovery further fueled debates among scientists about whether viruses are living organisms.

cau_hoi: The cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) technique, which earned three scientists the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017, allows what?
C: Capturing detailed structures of biological molecules that are frozen extremely quickly, without the need to create crystals
giai_thich: Biological molecules are frozen so quickly that the water around them turns into "glass ice" without forming crystals, preserving their natural shape. Computers stitch together hundreds of thousands of blurry images into sharp three-dimensional models. In 2020, cryo-EM helped determine the spike protein structure of the SARS-CoV-2 virus in just a few weeks, aiding vaccine development.

cau_hoi: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for the technique of "super-resolution" microscopy. What limit does this technique overcome?
C: The diffraction limit of light, about 0.2 nanometers
giai_thich: In 1873, Ernst Abbe pointed out that optical microscopes cannot distinguish two points closer than about half the wavelength of light. Eric Betzig, Stefan Hell, and William Moerner used controllable on-off fluorescent molecules to capture details much smaller than this limit in living cells. This allows us to observe individual protein molecules moving inside the cell.

cau_hoi: According to studies, the genetic code is "almost universal" with some minor exceptions. Where is the famous exception found in human cells?
D: Mitochondria, where the codon UGA codes for the amino acid tryptophan instead of being a stop signal
giai_thich: Mitochondria have their own translation system inherited from ancestral bacteria, and through evolution, have changed the meaning of some codons. In human mitochondria, UGA codes for tryptophan, and AUA codes for methionine instead of isoleucine. Some bacteria and flagellates also have their own "dialects" of the genetic code. These exceptions show that the genetic code can still change throughout the history of life.

cau_hoi: What is special about the hepatitis D virus compared to other hepatitis viruses?
B: Can only replicate when the patient is simultaneously infected with hepatitis B virus
giai_thich: Hepatitis D virus (delta) is a "satellite virus" with a very small RNA, about 1,700 bases, similar to viroids, and must borrow the protein coat of the hepatitis B virus. People infected with both viruses often suffer from more severe liver disease. Therefore, vaccination against hepatitis B also helps prevent hepatitis D. Vietnam vaccinates newborns against hepatitis B within 24 hours of birth.

cau_hoi: In 2015, the archaeal group "Asgard" (such as Lokiarchaeota) was discovered in deep-sea sediments near "Loki's Castle." Why are they important?
A: They are the closest known relatives of the ancestors of eukaryotes, such as humans, fungi, and plants
C: They are the most dangerous pathogenic bacteria
giai_thich: DNA found near the hydrothermal vent "Loki's Castle" between Greenland and Norway shows that these archaea have many genes previously thought to exist only in eukaryotes, such as genes that create the cell cytoskeleton. The groups are named after Norse gods: Loki, Thor, Odin, Heimdall. In 2020, a Japanese group successfully cultured an Asgard species for the first time after 12 years of persistence.

cau_hoi: "Cable bacteria" were discovered in marine sediment with what extraordinary ability?
C: To connect thousands of cells into long filaments several centimeters long, conducting electricity like cables
giai_thich: These bacteria connect end to end to form filaments up to several centimeters long. Cells deep down take electrons from hydrogen sulfide, transferring them up the filament to cells above, where there is oxygen to receive the electrons, like a live electrical wire. Danish scientists discovered them in 2012 when they observed a mysterious current running through the mud. They may help create new biologically conductive materials.

cau_hoi: Geobacter bacteria can "breathe" metals and generate electricity thanks to which structure?
giai_thich: Geobacter lives in oxygen-deprived soil and sediments, transferring electrons from organic matter it consumes to external iron minerals through nanowires. When placed in a "microbial fuel cell," it can generate a small current from wastewater. Scientists also use Geobacter to clean up uranium-contaminated soil.

cau_hoi: The bacterium Desulforudis audaxviator, discovered in 2008 at a depth of about 2.8 km in a South African gold mine, is special for what reason?
A: It is the only species living in that ecosystem, surviving on energy from radioactive decay in the rock
giai_thich: At that depth, there is no light or oxygen. Energy comes from reactions caused by natural radioactivity in the rock that splits water into hydrogen, which the bacteria use to survive. Almost all organisms in the water sample are a single species, doing everything on their own. Its name is derived from a line in Jules Verne's novel "Journey to the Center of the Earth": "Descend, O brave traveler."

cau_hoi: In 2020, Japanese and American scientists "awoke" microorganisms from marine sediments that are approximately how many years old?
giai_thich: The sample was drilled from the seabed of the South Pacific, where nutrient-poor sediments have accumulated slowly since the time of the dinosaurs. When fed, many microorganisms in the sample began to eat and reproduce again. Scientists believe they have lived at an extremely slow metabolic rate for tens of millions of years, almost "asleep." This expands our understanding of the limits of life.

cau_hoi: Choanoflagellates, single-celled organisms living in water, are of particular interest to scientists for what reason?
A: They are a dangerous type of virus
B: They are the ancestors of plants
C: They are the closest living unicellular relatives of animals
giai_thich: Choanoflagellates have a flagellum surrounded by a "collar" of microvilli, resembling the collar cells of sponges. Some species live in small colonies. Their genome contains many genes previously thought to exist only in animals, such as genes that help cells stick together. Studying them helps understand how the first multicellular animals emerged over 600 million years ago.

cau_hoi: According to scientists, how many times has multicellular life evolved independently in Earth's history?
A: Many times, estimated to be more than 20 times in different groups
giai_thich: Multicellularity has appeared independently in animals, plants, fungi, red algae, brown algae, slime molds, and some bacteria. However, "complex" multicellularity with many types of specialized tissues and organs has only appeared in a few groups such as animals, vascular plants, fungi, red algae, and brown algae. This suggests that the transition to multicellularity is not too rare, but building complex bodies is much more challenging.

cau_hoi: The technique of "optogenetics" allows for the control of nerve cells using light by introducing proteins derived from where?
D: From unicellular green algae (light-sensitive channelrhodopsin protein)
giai_thich: Chlamydomonas algae use channelrhodopsin in their "eyespot" to swim towards light. By introducing the gene for this protein into mouse nerve cells, scientists can use blue light transmitted through optical fibers to activate those cells in an instant. Since 2005, optogenetics has helped study the roles of different groups of nerve cells in memory, fear, and movement. In 2021, it even helped a blind patient regain part of their vision.

cau_hoi: In 2017, scientists stored a movie, a computer operating system, and many other files in DNA. Theoretically, how much data can 1 gram of DNA store?
giai_thich: Digital information consisting of 0s and 1s is converted into sequences of bases A, T, G, X, and then synthesized into DNA. Yaniv Erlich and Dina Zielinski managed to store many files and read them back without a single bit error. DNA is extremely durable when kept dry and cold: DNA from mammoths over a million years old is still readable. The current limitation is that the cost of synthesizing and reading DNA is still high, and the writing speed is slow.

cau_hoi: What principle does the "gene drive" technology being researched to combat malaria operate on?
C: Making a gene passed on to nearly all offspring instead of half, spreading quickly through the mosquito population
giai_thich: According to Mendel, each normal gene is passed on to about 50% of offspring. Gene drives use CRISPR to copy the gene to the other chromosome, so nearly 100% of offspring carry that gene. Scientists design gene drives to make female mosquitoes sterile or unable to transmit malaria parasites. Because it can change an entire species in nature, this technology needs to be evaluated very carefully before being released into the wild.

cau_hoi: Between 1970 and 1972, what was the first achievement of scientist Har Gobind Khorana (an Indian-American)?
A: Complete chemical synthesis of an artificial gene
giai_thich: Khorana contributed to decoding genetics and received the Nobel Prize in 1968 along with Nirenberg and Holley. Later, his team synthesized a tRNA gene from yeast consisting of 77 bases from chemicals, and in 1976 created a functional artificial gene in bacteria. His work laid the foundation for DNA synthesis techniques used in research and vaccine production today.

cau_hoi: In 2020, American scientists created "xenobots." What are they?
B: Tiny "living robots" made from frog embryonic cells, designed by computers
giai_thich: Scientists used algorithms on supercomputers to design shapes, then assembled skin cells and heart muscle cells taken from African clawed frog embryos (Xenopus laevis) into small blocks under 1 mm. They move on their own, can push small particles into piles, and heal themselves. In 2021, xenobots even "reproduced" by gathering discrete cells into new xenobots. They self-destruct after about a week.

cau_hoi: At the end of 2024, a large group of scientists called for not creating any artificial organisms due to potential unpredictable dangers. What was it?
D: "Mirror life" – bacteria with molecules that are mirror images of normal life
giai_thich: The molecules of life have "handedness": proteins use left-handed amino acids, DNA uses right-handed sugars. A "mirror" bacterium with all reverse molecules might not be recognized by the immune system and predatory bacteria, and could spread uncontrollably. Although the technology is still years away, about 38 scientists, including some who have previously researched this direction, wrote in the journal Science recommending a halt.

cau_hoi: How does the "base editing" technique, developed by David Liu's group in 2016, differ from conventional CRISPR-Cas9?
B: Directly changes one DNA "letter" to another without cutting both DNA strands
giai_thich: Conventional CRISPR-Cas9 cuts both DNA strands, allowing the cell to repair itself, sometimes causing unintended errors. Base editing uses a "blunt" version of Cas9 combined with a chemical enzyme to precisely convert C to T or A to G. In 2019, this group also developed "prime editing" as a text editor. In 2025, a baby in the U.S. with a rare genetic disease was treated with base editing designed specifically for them.

cau_hoi: In 2019, scientists created "hachimoji" DNA. What is special about this type of DNA?
D: Uses 8 types of base "letters" instead of 4, capable of storing information and transcribing into RNA
giai_thich: "Hachimoji" in Japanese means "eight letters." In addition to A, T, G, C, Steven Benner's group added 4 artificial bases that pair with each other according to their own rules. Hachimoji DNA has a stable double helix structure and can be transcribed into RNA. Research suggests that life on other planets, for example, could use chemical "alphabets" different from life on Earth.

cau_hoi: In 2022, scientists announced the oldest DNA ever known, about 2 million years old, found where and indicating what?
C: In sediments in Greenland, indicating that there used to be forests with woolly mammoths and reindeer
giai_thich: Environmental DNA was taken from sediment layers at Cape København, in northern Greenland. DNA fragments indicate that about 2 million years ago, the area was much warmer, with birch and willow forests, along with woolly mammoths, reindeer, hares, and even jellyfish in the nearby sea. The DNA was preserved by adhering to clay minerals. This record breaks the previous record of mammoth DNA, which was over 1 million years old.

chu_de: "Organoids" that scientists grow in laboratories are what?
A: Tiny three-dimensional "organs" grown from stem cells, self-organizing like real organs
giai_thich: When grown under suitable conditions, stem cells self-organize into small clusters the size of a pea resembling intestines, livers, kidneys, or miniature brains. In 2013, Madeline Lancaster's group created the first "mini-brain." Organoids help study how the Zika virus harms fetal brains and test drugs tailored for individual cancer patients without needing to test on humans.

cau_hoi: Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes but can produce many more types of proteins. What is the main mechanism behind this?
A: Alternative splicing: one gene can produce multiple different mRNA versions
giai_thich: In 1977, Richard Roberts and Phillip Sharp discovered that genes are "interrupted": coding segments (exons) are interspersed with non-coding segments (introns). RNA removes introns and connects exons, allowing the cell to choose different combinations of exons. A gene in fruit flies, Dscam, can theoretically produce over 38,000 protein versions. Roberts and Sharp received the Nobel Prize in 1993.

cau_hoi: In 1989, Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering what about RNA?
A: RNA is not present in cells
B: RNA is only found in viruses
C: RNA can act as a catalyst like enzymes (called ribozymes)
giai_thich: Previously, it was believed that only proteins could act as enzymes. Cech discovered an RNA in the ciliate Tetrahymena that can self-cut and splice without the need for proteins. Altman found an RNA that cuts tRNA molecules. This discovery supports the "RNA world" hypothesis: early life may have used RNA to both store information and act as enzymes before DNA and proteins emerged.

cau_hoi: How does the protein kinesin transport "cargo" along microtubules in the cell?
B: "Walks" on two "feet", each step about 8 nanometers long, using one ATP molecule
giai_thich: Kinesin has two heads like two feet, alternately attaching to the microtubule and stepping forward, like a tightrope walker. Each step is about 8 nm, the exact distance between the units of the microtubule, and it can step about 100 times per second. In a neuron that is over a meter long, kinesin transports vesicles containing neurotransmitters from the cell body to the end of the axon.

cau_hoi: The enzyme ATP synthase, which produces most of the ATP in the cell, operates like which machine?
D: A rotating motor like a turbine, spinning when H⁺ ions flow through
giai_thich: In the inner membrane of mitochondria, the flow of protons through the base of ATP synthase causes a rotating shaft to spin, at a rate of about 100 revolutions per second. Each rotation forces ADP and phosphate molecules together, producing 3 ATP. Paul Boyer and John Walker received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1997 for deciphering this mechanism. In 1997, Japanese scientists even recorded a video showing its shaft spinning.

cau_hoi: The flagellum of the bacterium E. coli is propelled by a "motor" at its base. What is a characteristic of this motor?
B: Is a real rotating motor, capable of spinning hundreds to thousands of times per second
D: Does not rotate but only flaps
giai_thich: The flagellar motor consists of about 20 types of proteins, rotating due to the flow of ions through the cell membrane, similar to an electric motor. In E. coli, it spins about 100 times per second, while in some bacteria using sodium ions, it can reach about 1,700 times per second. When the motor changes direction, the flagella separate, causing the bacteria to tumble and change swimming direction.

cau_hoi: The archaeon Methanopyrus kandleri "Strain 116" holds what record published in 2008?
D: Reproduces at 122°C, the highest temperature ever recorded for life
giai_thich: Methanopyrus kandleri was collected from a hydrothermal vent at a depth of about 2,000 m off the coast of Japan. Under high pressure in the laboratory, it still reproduces at 122°C, surpassing the previous record of 121°C set by Strain 121. This organism produces methane from hydrogen and CO₂. Scientists believe the temperature limit for life may be around 130 – 150°C, as above that, molecules like DNA and ATP break down too quickly.

cau_hoi: In 2018, scientist He Jiankui (China) caused a global stir for doing what?
A: Editing human embryo genes using CRISPR, creating two twin girls, severely violating ethical rules
giai_thich: He claimed to have edited the CCR5 gene in embryos to make the girls resistant to HIV, but the actions were opaque, medically unnecessary, and posed risks of unintended mutations that could be inherited by future generations. The global scientific community condemned it strongly. In 2019, he was sentenced to 3 years in prison by a Chinese court. The event prompted countries to tighten regulations on human gene editing.

cau_hoi: Scientists estimate that there are about how many bacterial and archaeal cells on Earth?
giai_thich: The figure of 10³⁰ is larger than the number of stars in the observable universe (about 10²²) by millions of times. Most microorganisms live in deep soil, sediment, and oceans. If all bacteria were lined up, they could stretch beyond our galaxy. Despite their small size, they control the carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycles of the entire planet.

cau_hoi: The bacterium Pelagibacter ubique (SAR11 group) is considered the most abundant organism in the ocean. What is special about its genome?
C: Is one of the smallest genomes of free-living organisms, with almost no "extra" DNA
D: Is identical to the human genome
giai_thich: Pelagibacter has a genome of about 1.3 million base pairs with around 1,350 genes, maximally "streamlined" to survive in nutrient-poor seawater. The SAR11 group may account for about one-third of the cells in the ocean's surface layer, totaling about 2 × 10²⁸ cells. Despite being very common, it was only successfully cultured for the first time in 2002 due to its very peculiar nutritional requirements.
